lessons.title: What a Share Actually Is
lessons.keyIdea: A share is a residual claim on a business — last in line, unlimited on the upside, and capped at zero on the downside.

blocks.text: People buy shares long before anyone tells them what a share is. The price moves, the app shows a green number, and the question of what was actually purchased never comes up. It is worth answering properly, because almost everything else in this track follows from it.
A unit of ownership in a company. Owning one makes you a part-owner of the business itself — not a lender to it, and not a customer of it.

That ownership is real but limited. It does not entitle you to walk into the company and take a desk. It entitles you to two things: a vote on certain decisions, and a claim on whatever value is left over after everyone else has been paid.

The phrase "left over" is doing the work in that sentence. A company pays its suppliers, its staff, its lenders and its tax bill first. Shareholders are last in the queue. What reaches them is the residual.
A claim on what remains after all other obligations are met. Shareholders hold one; lenders do not.

A company earns 100 in revenue. Suppliers take 40, staff take 35, interest on debt takes 10, and tax takes 5. The residual is 10, and it belongs to the shareholders — either paid out or reinvested on their behalf. If revenue had been 90 instead, the first four claims would still take 90, and the residual would be zero.

This is why share prices move so much more than a company's revenue does. The residual is the thin layer at the end of a stack, so a small change in the size of the stack is a large change in the layer. A 10% fall in revenue in that example does not reduce the shareholders' claim by 10%. It removes it entirely.

Being last in the queue sounds like a bad deal, and on the downside it is. The compensation sits on the other side: the residual has no ceiling. A lender who is owed 10 receives 10 whether the company earns 100 or 100,000. The shareholders receive everything above the obligations, however large that becomes.

So a share is an asymmetric instrument. Bounded loss, unbounded gain. That asymmetry is the single most important structural fact about equities, and it is what makes them behave so differently from the currency pairs in the Forex track, where both sides of a position are open-ended.

The lower bound comes from a legal arrangement most people never think about, and it is not a natural feature of ownership. If you own a corner shop outright and it fails owing money, the creditors can pursue you personally. If you own shares in a company that fails owing money, they cannot.
The rule that a shareholder's loss is capped at what they paid for the shares. Creditors of the company have no claim on the shareholder's other assets.

Limited liability caps what you can lose on one company. It does not cap what you can lose overall, and it does not apply if you borrow to buy the shares. Money borrowed on margin is still owed after the shares are worthless — the loss stops at zero for the share, not for you. Chapter 3 covers this properly.

What the vote buys you is worth being realistic about. In theory shareholders elect the board and the board hires the management. In practice a holding of a few hundred shares in a company with billions outstanding is not a meaningful lever, and most private investors never vote at all.

This matters for how you should think about a share you hold. You are not going to influence the business. You are making a judgment about whether the residual claim you bought is worth what you paid for it — and, in the next lesson, whether that judgment is the kind that has an edge behind it.

Two people put 1,000 into the same company on the same day. One buys shares. One lends the company 1,000 at 6% interest. Over five years the company does extremely well. The lender receives 60 a year and their 1,000 back — exactly what was agreed, and not a unit more. The shareholder receives whatever the residual has become, which may be far more, or nothing.

One consequence is that the two positions are wrong in different ways. The lender is wrong when the company cannot pay, which is rare and severe. The shareholder is wrong far more often and usually less severely — but their claim can be wiped out while the company survives, because the residual can go to zero without the obligations going unpaid.
Keep that distinction in view. "The company is fine" and "the shares are fine" are different statements, and Chapter 5 has case studies where they came apart badly.
One complication is worth knowing before you own anything, because it changes what the vote is worth.
A category of share within the same company. Different classes can carry different voting rights while having an identical claim on the profits.

Some companies issue more than one class. A founder may hold shares carrying ten votes each while the shares sold to the public carry one, or none at all. The economic claim is usually the same, so both classes rise and fall together. The control is not.

If a company has multiple share classes, check which one you are buying and what it can vote on. This is not usually a reason to avoid the company. It is a reason to stop imagining the vote is your protection, and to judge the position purely on whether the business will be worth more later.

blocks.text: What to look for when you next open a holding. Confirm three things, in this order.

First, whether you own shares in a company at all, or units in a fund that owns shares. These behave differently and Lesson 5 explains why. Second, if it is a single company, whether the class you hold votes. Third, where the company sits in the queue you met above: how much it owes, and to whom, because everything owed is paid before anything reaches you.

Two companies each earn a residual of 10 on revenue of 100. The first has no debt. The second pays 20 a year in interest before reaching that 10. If revenue falls 15% at both, the first still has a residual. The second has none, and its shareholders own the leftover of a number that no longer exists.

Take any company whose shares you could buy. Find its most recent annual figures and write down four numbers: revenue, total costs, interest paid, and what remained. Then write down what a 10% fall in revenue would do to the last number if the first three were unchanged. That single calculation explains more about why the share price moves than any chart you will look at this month.

quiz.question: A company's revenue falls by 10%, and its obligations to suppliers, staff, lenders and tax are unchanged. What happens to the shareholders' claim?
options: It falls by 10%, in proportion to revenue
It falls by more than 10%, because the residual absorbs the whole shortfall
It is unchanged, because shareholders are paid first
It falls by 10% only if the company chooses to pay a smaller dividend
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Shareholders hold the residual — what is left after fixed obligations. Because those obligations do not shrink with revenue, the whole shortfall lands on the residual, so the shareholders' claim moves by much more than revenue does. This is why share prices are more volatile than the businesses underneath them.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. Shareholders are last in the queue, not first, and the obligations ahead of them do not fall just because revenue did. The entire shortfall comes out of the residual, so the shareholders' claim falls by considerably more than 10%.

quiz.question: A company you own shares in is sold, and after all debts are repaid there is cash left over. Who has a claim on it?
options: The lenders, because they rank first in every situation
The shareholders, because a residual claim is a claim on whatever remains after all obligations are met
The staff and suppliers, in proportion to what they were paid
Nobody — surplus cash returns to the government
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Ranking last means being paid only after everyone else, which is the downside. The compensation is that once everyone else has been paid in full, whatever remains belongs entirely to shareholders — and there is no ceiling on how large it can be.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. Lenders, staff and suppliers are owed fixed amounts and are paid first, but they are owed only those amounts. Anything remaining after every obligation is met belongs to the shareholders — that is what a residual claim means.

quiz.question: A company issues two share classes with identical claims on profits, but one carries ten votes per share and the other carries one. What follows for someone buying the one-vote class?
options: They will receive a smaller share of any dividend
Their economic claim is the same, but the vote is not a meaningful protection, so the position rests entirely on whether the business becomes more valuable
The two classes will trade at completely unrelated prices
They cannot sell the shares without the founder's approval
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The claim on profits is identical, so the two classes rise and fall broadly together. What differs is control, and control was never realistic for a small holder anyway. The honest conclusion is to stop treating the vote as protection and judge the holding purely on the business.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. Different voting rights do not usually mean a different claim on profits, and they place no restriction on selling. What changes is who controls the company — which means the vote is not your protection, and the position stands or falls on the business itself.

keyTerms.def: A unit of ownership in a company — a part-owner, not a lender.
A claim on what is left after suppliers, staff, lenders and tax are paid. Shareholders hold one.
The rule capping a shareholder's loss at what they paid for the shares.

lessons.title: Investing vs Gambling
lessons.keyIdea: The difference is not how risky it feels. It is whether the activity is positive-sum before costs, and who is on the other side.

blocks.text: The usual answer is that investing is sensible and gambling is reckless, or that investing is slow and gambling is fast. Neither survives contact with reality. Buying a single speculative company with your savings is investing by that definition, and it is plainly a gamble. A structured bet with a known edge is gambling by that definition, and it is plainly not reckless.
The honest distinction is structural, and it has two parts: where the return comes from, and who is on the other side of you.
An activity where the total value held by all participants can grow, because value is being created outside the transactions themselves.
An activity where one participant's gain is exactly another's loss. Nothing is created; the pot is only redistributed.

Owning shares in productive businesses is positive-sum. The companies employ people, sell things, and generate cash. That cash accrues to the residual claim you learned about in Lesson 1. If every shareholder in the world held their shares and did nothing, they could still collectively be better off in ten years, because the businesses underneath produced something.

A roulette wheel is not like this. The wheel produces nothing. Every unit won by one player is a unit lost by another, minus the house edge — which makes it negative-sum for the players taken together.

Short-term trading in shares is much closer to the roulette wheel than to ownership. Over a holding period of minutes or days, the businesses underneath have produced almost nothing. Nearly all of what you gain in that window comes from another trader, minus costs — so the activity is close to zero-sum before fees and negative-sum after them. The asset being productive does not make every activity involving it productive.

This is where the second part matters: who is on the other side. Someone is taking the opposite side of every trade you place, and in a liquid market that someone is usually a firm whose entire business is being better at this than you are.

It is worth knowing what actually happens to people who do this seriously, rather than guessing. The evidence here is unusually good, because Taiwan's stock exchange gave researchers a complete record of every trade and every trader for years at a time — something no other market has published at that granularity.

Barber, Lee, Liu and Odean studied the complete transaction records of the Taiwan Stock Exchange. In a typical six-month period, more than 80% of day traders lost money after costs. In the follow-up work published in the Review of Asset Pricing Studies (2020, volume 10, issue 1, pages 61 to 93), they found that profitable and unprofitable traders were almost equally likely to keep trading the following year — roughly 96% against 95%. Losing money did not, in practice, stop people.

Two things in that finding deserve attention. The first is the loss rate itself. The second, and more useful one, is that the losses did not teach. If the experience of losing reliably corrected the behaviour, the population of day traders would improve over time. It largely did not.

You will see the figure "90% of day traders lose money" repeated constantly, usually with no source attached. The carefully measured number from complete exchange records is "more than 80% in a typical six-month period" — which is a different and more precise claim. When a striking statistic circulates without a traceable source, treat the statistic itself as the thing to check first. That habit is worth more than the number.

So the test is not whether an activity feels risky. It is a pair of questions you can ask about anything: is value being created outside the transaction, and do I have a reason to believe I am better informed than whoever is on the other side?

Buying a diversified basket of productive companies and holding it for twenty years passes the first test comfortably and makes the second largely irrelevant, because you are not trying to beat anyone. Trading in and out of single companies on the strength of a news headline fails both.

Two people each put 5,000 into the market on the same morning. One buys a broad index fund and does not look at it again for a decade. The other trades it actively, in and out, forty times a year. Ignoring skill entirely, they face completely different structures: the first collects whatever the underlying businesses produced, minus a small fee. The second collects whatever the businesses produced, minus a small fee, minus forty rounds of spread and commission, plus or minus whatever they gained or lost against the other side of each trade.

The second is not necessarily doomed. It is carrying a cost the first is not, and it needs a genuine edge just to break even against the first. Chapter 4 puts real numbers on what that costs over a lifetime.

None of this makes shares safe. Foundations Chapter 2 made the point that being right often is not the same as trading well, and it holds here: the positive-sum nature of ownership is a statement about the long run and about diversified baskets, not a promise about any single company or any single year.
The two questions can be turned into arithmetic, which is more useful than the labels.
The average result of an activity if it were repeated many times: each possible outcome multiplied by its probability, all added together.

A European roulette wheel has 37 pockets. A bet on a single number pays 35 to 1. Multiply the outcomes by their probabilities and the expected value of every unit staked is about 0.973 units returned — a loss of 2.7% per spin, on average, forever. Nothing about the player changes that figure. It is a property of the wheel.

Stake 1 unit on one number. You win 35 units with probability 1 in 37, and lose 1 unit with probability 36 in 37. The average outcome is (35 divided by 37) minus (36 divided by 37), which is about minus 0.027. Repeat it a thousand times and the average result is a loss of about 27 units, regardless of any streak along the way.

A diversified holding of productive companies has no equivalent fixed edge working against it. Its expected return is uncertain and can be negative over any given decade, but the source of the return is the cash the companies generate rather than another participant's loss. That is the whole of the distinction, and it says nothing about safety.

Positive expected value is not a guarantee and it is not comfort. It says the average of many repetitions is favourable. You get one life, not many repetitions, which is exactly why position sizing exists and why Chapter 3 spends a chapter on it.

blocks.text: What to look for, applied to any activity someone describes as investing. Ask where the money comes from if you win. If the answer is that a business produced it, the activity is ownership. If the answer is that another participant lost it, the activity is a wager however respectable its packaging. And if the answer is that later entrants pay earlier ones, the activity is neither and you should leave.

Take one thing you have considered buying — a share, a fund, a currency, a token. Write one sentence answering where a gain would come from. If you cannot complete the sentence without referring to someone else selling to you at a higher price, you have identified a zero-sum position, and it needs an edge rather than patience.

quiz.question: What is the structural difference between long-term share ownership and a casino game?
options: Share ownership is less risky, because share prices cannot fall to zero
Share ownership is positive-sum — the businesses underneath produce value — while the casino game only redistributes what players bring
Share ownership is slower, and slower activities are safer
There is no real difference; both are bets on an uncertain outcome
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The return from owning productive businesses comes from value created outside the transactions themselves, so all holders can gain together. A casino game creates nothing, so one player's gain is another's loss minus the house edge. Note that this defence applies to long-term ownership — short-term trading in the same shares is close to zero-sum before costs.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. It is not about speed or about how risky it feels, and share prices certainly can fall to zero. The difference is that productive businesses create value outside the transactions, so ownership is positive-sum, whereas a casino game only redistributes what players bring, minus the house edge.

quiz.question: Why is the expected value of a single-number roulette bet negative no matter how skilled the player is?
options: Because casinos change the odds for skilled players
Because the wheel has 37 pockets while the payout is 35 to 1, so the shortfall is built into the game itself
Because players tend to bet too much on each spin
Because winnings are taxed
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The average return is about 0.973 units for every unit staked, a loss of roughly 2.7% per spin. It is a property of the wheel, not of the player, which is why no amount of skill or discipline changes it.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. The negative expectation comes from the structure of the game: 37 possible outcomes paying 35 to 1. Nothing the player does alters that, which is precisely what distinguishes it from owning productive assets.

quiz.question: Short-term trading in shares is closest in structure to which of the following, and why?
options: Long-term ownership, since the same shares are involved
A zero-sum wager, because over minutes or days the underlying businesses have not changed and your gain comes from another participant
A savings account, because shares are regulated
A lottery, because outcomes are entirely random
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The instrument is the same but the source of return is not. Over a holding period of minutes, the businesses have generated nothing new, so any gain comes from whoever took the other side — before costs, which make the activity negative-sum in aggregate.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. What matters is where the return comes from, not what is being traded. Over minutes or days the companies have produced nothing new, so the gain must come from another participant — and costs make that a losing proposition on average.

keyTerms.def: An activity where all participants can gain together, because value is created outside the transactions.
An activity where one participant's gain is exactly another's loss.

lessons.title: How Shares Are Priced and Traded
lessons.keyIdea: There is no single price. There is a highest bid, a lowest offer, and a gap between them that you pay every time you cross it.

blocks.text: An app shows one number and calls it the price. That number is a summary of something more detailed, and the detail is where your costs live.
Behind it is an order book: a live list of everyone currently willing to buy, with the price each will pay, and everyone currently willing to sell, with the price each will accept.
The highest price anyone is currently willing to pay for the share.
The lowest price anyone is currently willing to sell it for. Also called the offer.
The gap between the bid and the ask. It is a real cost, paid at the moment of trading rather than billed separately.

A share shows a bid of 24.98 and an ask of 25.02. The quoted price is 25.00 — the midpoint, which is a number nobody is actually offering. Buy now and you pay 25.02. Sell immediately afterwards and you receive 24.98. You are down 0.04 per share, or 0.16%, without the price having moved at all.

That 0.16% is the entry fee for a round trip. Pay it once a decade and it is irrelevant. Pay it forty times a year, as the active trader in the previous lesson did, and it becomes one of the largest costs you face — which is exactly why the arithmetic there was so unforgiving.

Readers who took the Forex track have met this already, in Chapter 1 Lesson 4. The mechanism is identical; only the units differ. Currency traders count it in pips, share traders count it in cents, and both are paying the same thing.
You control whether you pay it, through the type of order you place.
An instruction to trade immediately at whatever price is currently available. Certain to execute, uncertain in price.
An instruction to trade only at a stated price or better. Certain in price, uncertain whether it executes at all.

A market order crosses the spread on purpose: you take the best price on offer and accept the 0.04. A limit order sits in the book and waits for someone to come to you. If they do, you avoid the spread. If they do not, you simply do not trade — and if the price runs away in the meantime, not trading may have cost more than the spread would have.

The spread is not fixed. It widens when few people are trading — early morning, late afternoon, holidays, and above all during the sharp moves when you are most likely to want out. Forex Chapter 5's case studies are the extreme version of this: in a genuine liquidity vacuum the book can empty, and a market order fills at a price far from the last one quoted. A market order is a promise to execute, never a promise about the price.
Once the trade matches, ownership does not change hands instantly. There is a settlement period between agreeing the trade and the shares and money actually moving.
The process of actually exchanging shares for money after a trade is agreed. It happens a set number of business days after the trade date.

In the United States that period is one business day. The Securities and Exchange Commission shortened it from two days to one under Exchange Act Rule 15c6-1(a), effective 28 May 2024. The convention is written as T+1 — trade date plus one business day.

The stated purpose was to reduce the risk that builds up while a trade is agreed but not yet completed. A shorter window means less time for either side to fail, and less exposure to price movement in between.

You sell shares on a Monday under T+1. The trade is agreed on Monday at Monday's price, and the cash settles on Tuesday. If you sell on a Friday, settlement lands on the following Monday, because the count is in business days and the weekend does not count.

Settlement looks like plumbing, and for a long-term holder it is. It becomes visible at exactly two moments: when you need the cash by a specific date, and when a market is under stress. Chapter 5 covers January 2021, when settlement mechanics stopped being invisible and became the story.

The practical takeaway is small and worth keeping. There is no single price — there is a bid, an ask, and a gap you pay to cross. You choose whether to cross it. And the trade you agree today is not finished until it settles.
Two further order types appear in most trading applications, and both are frequently misunderstood.
An instruction that becomes a market order once the price reaches a stated level. It does not guarantee a price — only that an order is sent.

The distinction between a stop order and a limit order is where beginners lose money without understanding how. A stop order at 45 does not sell at 45. It sends a market order once 45 trades, and that order fills at whatever the book offers next, which in a fast fall may be well below.

You place a stop to sell at 45. Bad news arrives overnight and the share opens at 38. The stop triggers immediately and sells near 38, not 45. Nothing malfunctioned. The order did exactly what it says, and what it says is different from what most people assume it says.

The spread and the depth behind it are separate things. A share can show a narrow spread with very little volume behind the best prices, so a larger order eats through several levels and achieves an average price far from the quote. Check the volume traded, not only the spread.
How easily an asset can be bought or sold in reasonable size without moving its price. High volume and a narrow spread together indicate it; either alone does not.

blocks.text: What to look for before placing any order. Convert the spread to a percentage of the price, because a 4 cent spread means one thing on a 25 share and something very different on a 2 share. Check the average daily volume against the size you intend to trade. Avoid the first and last few minutes of the trading session, when spreads are widest. And use a limit order by default, accepting that it may not execute.

Look up any share you follow and record the bid, the ask and the last price at two moments: shortly after the market opens, and in the middle of the session. Calculate the spread as a percentage of the midpoint each time. The difference between the two readings is a cost you would have paid without ever seeing it itemised.

quiz.question: A share is quoted with a bid of 40.90 and an ask of 41.10. You buy with a market order and sell again a minute later with another market order, and the book has not moved. What is the result?
options: You break even, because the price did not change
You lose 0.20 per share — you bought at the ask and sold at the bid
You gain 0.20 per share, because you captured the spread
It depends on the commission only; the spread does not affect you
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. A market order crosses the spread, so you bought at 41.10 and sold at 40.90 — a loss of 0.20 per share, close to 0.5% of the value, on an unchanged market. Crossing the spread twice is what a round trip costs, before any commission at all.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. Market orders take whatever is available, so you buy at the ask (41.10) and sell at the bid (40.90). That is a loss of 0.20 per share even though the quoted price never moved. Only a resting limit order can avoid paying the spread — at the risk of not trading at all.

quiz.question: You place a stop order to sell at 45. Overnight news causes the share to open at 38. What happens?
options: The order sells at 45, since that is the price you specified
The order sells near 38, because a stop becomes a market order once triggered and fills at whatever is available
The order is cancelled because 45 never traded
The order sells at the midpoint of 45 and 38
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. A stop order specifies a trigger, not a price. Once the level is reached it sends a market order, which fills at whatever the book offers — in a gap down, well below the stop level. This is the single most common misunderstanding about protective orders.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. A stop order does not guarantee the stop price. It guarantees that an order is sent once the level is reached, and that order then fills at whatever prices are actually available, which after a gap can be far lower.

quiz.question: A share shows a narrow bid-ask spread but very low average daily volume. What risk does this create for a larger order?
options: None, since a narrow spread means the trade will be cheap
The order may eat through several price levels, achieving an average price well away from the quote
The trade will be rejected by the exchange
The settlement period will be longer than usual
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The quote shows only the best prices, not how much size sits behind them. With thin volume, an order larger than the top of the book fills at progressively worse prices — so liquidity requires both a narrow spread and real volume, not either alone.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. The spread describes the gap between the best bid and best ask; it says nothing about how many shares are available at those prices. Thin volume means a large order works through worse and worse levels.

keyTerms.def: The highest price anyone is currently willing to pay.
The lowest price anyone is currently willing to sell for.
The gap between bid and ask — a real cost paid when you trade, not billed separately.
Trade immediately at the best available price. Certain to execute, uncertain in price.
Trade only at a stated price or better. Certain in price, uncertain to execute.
The exchange of shares for money after a trade is agreed — T+1 in the United States since 28 May 2024.

lessons.title: What Is an Index?
lessons.keyIdea: An index is a rule for combining chosen shares into one number. Change the rule and the same market tells a different story.

blocks.text: News reports say "the market rose 1% today" as though the market were a single thing with a single price. It is not. What rose was an index, and an index is a construction: somebody chose which companies to include and how much weight to give each one.
A rule for combining the prices of a chosen set of shares into one number, so the group can be tracked over time.

Two decisions define any index. Which companies are in it, and how the contribution of each is weighted. The second decision is the one almost nobody examines, and it changes the answer more than people expect.
The most common method weights each company by its market value, so bigger companies move the index more.
Weighting each company by its total market value, so a company worth twice as much has twice the influence on the index.

The S&P 500 uses a refinement of this called float adjustment. It counts only the shares actually available for the public to buy, excluding blocks held by governments, founders and other companies. The reasoning is that shares nobody can purchase should not affect a measure of what the investable market is doing.

The index level is then the total float-adjusted market value of the constituents, divided by a number called the divisor. The divisor exists so that mechanical events — a stock split, a company joining or leaving — do not make the index jump when nothing real has happened. S&P Dow Jones Indices publishes both the index-mathematics and float-adjustment methodologies openly, which is worth knowing: the rule is not a secret, and you can read it.
The other main method is older and stranger.
Weighting each company by its share price alone, regardless of the size of the company.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average works this way. It adds the share prices of its 30 companies and divides by its own divisor. The consequence is that influence tracks the price per share and not the size of the business.

One company trades at 300 a share, another at 100. In a price-weighted index the first has three times the influence of the second — even if the second company is worth far more in total, because it has issued many more shares. A 1% move in the 300 share moves the index three times as much as a 1% move in the 100 share.

Share price on its own says nothing about the size of a company. A company can halve its share price tomorrow by splitting its shares two-for-one, without anything about the business changing. In a price-weighted index that split permanently reduces the company's influence. This is why price weighting is generally regarded as a historical artefact rather than a good design — it was easy to compute in 1896, when the arithmetic was done by hand.

So "the market" depends on which index you mean. A day when a few very large companies fall and most smaller ones rise can be a down day for a cap-weighted index and an up day for an equally-weighted one covering the same companies. Neither number is lying. They are answering different questions.
This is worth carrying into the next lesson, because when you buy an index fund you are not buying "the market". You are buying a specific rule, and you should know which one.

A cap-weighted index of the same 500 companies concentrates: if the largest handful grow to a third of the total value, a third of your return depends on those few. An equal-weighted version of the identical list gives each company the same share, so it leans more on the smaller members. Same companies, same day, different number.

Cap weighting has one consequence worth stating plainly, because it surprises people who believe an index fund is automatically diversified. The weights are not fixed. They move with price, so whatever has risen most owns the largest share of the index — and it owns that share precisely because it has already risen.

This means a cap-weighted index concentrates on its own. Nobody decides to increase the weighting of the most expensive part of the market; the rule does it automatically as prices rise. An index of 500 companies can quietly become a bet on a handful of them. Chapter 5 looks at what that produced in 1999, and it is the strongest honest caveat against treating a broad index fund as risk-free diversification.

That is a caveat, not an argument against index funds. The alternatives have their own weighting problems, and the fee arithmetic in Lesson 7 is a powerful counterweight. The point is only that you should know what the rule does when prices move, rather than assuming a large number of holdings guarantees spread.

One last thing an index quietly omits. Most headline indices are price indices — they track share prices only, and ignore dividends paid along the way. Total return versions exist and are usually higher. Lesson 6 covers why that difference is larger than it sounds.
There is a third weighting method, less common but useful because it isolates what the other two are doing.
Giving every company in the index the same weight regardless of its size or share price, and restoring those weights periodically.

An equal-weighted version of the same 500 companies gives the smallest constituent exactly the influence of the largest. It therefore tells you what the typical company did, while the cap-weighted version tells you what the typical unit of money did. Those two questions have different answers, and in a market led by a handful of very large companies they can differ substantially over a year.

Suppose the ten largest companies rise 20% and the other 490 fall 2%. A cap-weighted index dominated by those ten can show a solid gain. An equal-weighted index of the identical companies shows a small loss. Neither is wrong, and headlines quote only the first.
Indices also change their membership, and the change is not free.
The periodic review in which an index provider adds and removes companies according to its published rules.

Every fund tracking an index must trade when the index reconstitutes, and it must do so at roughly the same time as every other tracker. Those trades cost money, paid out of the fund. This is one reason a fund never quite matches its index, which is the tracking difference the next lesson defines.

blocks.text: What to look for before treating any index number as information. Find out how many companies it holds, how it weights them, how concentrated the top ten are as a share of the whole, and whether the figure quoted is a price index or a total return index. Those four facts change the meaning of the number more than the number itself does.

Find the fact sheet for any broad index fund and locate the combined weight of its ten largest holdings. Write the figure down. Then decide honestly whether you would have chosen to put that proportion of your money into those ten companies as a deliberate decision. The rule made that choice for you, and the fact sheet is where you find out what it chose.

quiz.question: Company A trades at 300 a share and is worth 10 billion in total. Company B trades at 50 a share and is worth 80 billion. Which has more influence on a price-weighted index like the Dow?
options: Company B, because it is the larger company
Company A, because price weighting counts the share price and ignores company size
They have equal influence, because indices treat members equally
Company B, because it has more shares outstanding
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Price weighting looks only at the price per share, so A has six times the influence of B despite being an eighth of the size. A cap-weighted index would do the opposite. This is exactly why it matters which rule an index uses before you read anything into its movement.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. A price-weighted index adds share prices and divides — it never looks at how large the company is. Company A at 300 a share has six times the influence of Company B at 50, even though B is eight times the business. Size only drives the weighting in a market-capitalisation index.

quiz.question: The ten largest companies in an index rise 20% while the remaining 490 fall 2%. What does this do to a cap-weighted index compared with an equal-weighted one covering the same companies?
options: Both show the same result, since the companies are identical
The cap-weighted index can show a clear gain while the equal-weighted one shows a small loss
The equal-weighted index rises more, because it holds more small companies
Neither moves, because the gains and losses cancel out
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Cap weighting tells you what the typical unit of money did; equal weighting tells you what the typical company did. When a small number of very large companies lead, those two answers diverge — and the headline always quotes the first.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. The same companies can produce very different index results depending on the weighting rule. Cap weighting is dominated by the largest constituents, so a rise concentrated in the top ten can outweigh a broad decline across the other 490.

quiz.question: Why does index reconstitution create a cost for the funds that track the index?
options: The index provider charges investors a fee at each review
Every tracking fund must buy the additions and sell the removals at roughly the same time, and those trades cost money paid out of the fund
Reconstitution triggers a tax charge for all holders
Funds must be closed and reopened when the index changes
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Tracking a rule means following it, including when it changes membership. Many funds trading the same names at the same moment is an expensive way to trade, and the cost comes out of fund assets — one of the reasons a fund never matches its index exactly.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. The cost is a trading cost, not a fee or a tax. Trackers must all buy the new constituents and sell the departing ones around the same date, and that concentrated trading is paid for out of the fund itself.

keyTerms.def: A rule for combining chosen shares into a single trackable number.
Weighting each company by its market value; used by the S&P 500, float-adjusted.
Weighting by share price alone, regardless of company size; used by the Dow.
A number an index is divided by so splits and membership changes do not create artificial jumps.

lessons.title: What Is an ETF?
lessons.keyIdea: A fund that trades like a share. A creation and redemption mechanism is what stops its price drifting away from what it holds.

blocks.text: An index is a rule. An exchange-traded fund is a way to own the thing the rule describes, in one purchase, on an exchange.
A fund holding a basket of assets, whose own shares trade on an exchange throughout the day like an ordinary share.

Buy one share of a broad index ETF and you own a small slice of every company in that index, in the proportions the index rule specifies. That is the appeal: diversification in a single transaction, at a cost that Lesson 7 will put numbers to.

This raises an obvious problem. The ETF's own share price is set by supply and demand on the exchange, minute by minute. The value of what it actually holds is a separate number. What stops the two drifting apart?
The value of everything the fund holds, divided by the number of fund shares outstanding — what one share is actually backed by.
The answer is a mechanism most investors never see, run by a small set of large firms.
A large financial firm permitted to create new ETF shares or redeem existing ones by trading directly with the fund.

An authorised participant can do something you cannot. It can deliver the underlying basket of shares to the fund and receive newly created ETF shares in return, or hand back a block of ETF shares and receive the underlying basket. The US Securities and Exchange Commission describes this creation and redemption process in its investor bulletin on ETFs, and it is the structural feature that makes the whole thing work.
That ability turns any gap between the ETF price and its NAV into a profit opportunity, and pursuing the profit closes the gap.

An ETF is trading at 100.40 while the basket it holds is worth 100.00 a share. An authorised participant buys the underlying shares for 100.00, delivers them to the fund, receives new ETF shares, and sells them at 100.40. Doing this adds supply to the ETF and demand to the underlying, pushing the two prices together. The profit exists only while the gap does.

The SEC's own framing is that the market price is generally kept close to NAV because of this arbitrage function inherent in the structure. Note the word generally. It is a mechanism, not a guarantee.
An ETF trading above its NAV is at a premium; below it, a discount.

Premiums and discounts widen exactly when you would least want them to. If the underlying market is closed, illiquid or falling fast, an authorised participant cannot price or trade the basket reliably, and the arbitrage that normally closes the gap weakens. ETFs holding hard-to-trade assets — small foreign markets, corporate bonds — show this most. The mechanism is strongest in the calm conditions where you need it least.
A second thing worth checking is how the fund actually obtains its exposure.

Most funds hold the real securities, which is called physical replication. Some instead enter a contract with a bank that agrees to pay the index return, which is called synthetic replication. The synthetic version can track more closely and reach otherwise awkward markets — but it introduces a party who has to honour the contract.

Synthetic replication adds counterparty risk: a risk that is not about the index at all, but about whether the bank on the other side of the swap can pay. Foundations Chapter 2 made the general point that risks you have not named are the ones that hurt. This is a concrete instance — the fund can track the index perfectly and still fail for a reason that has nothing to do with the index.
Finally, no fund tracks its index exactly. Fees, trading costs, and the timing of dividends all cause small gaps.
The gap between a fund's return and its index's return over a period. Tracking error is the variability of that gap.

A fund with a slightly higher fee but tighter tracking can leave you better off than a cheaper one that lags. The advertised fee is the headline; the tracking difference is the result. Both are worth checking, and the next lesson explains why even small differences matter so much over time.
Two further features of a fund affect what you actually receive, and neither appears in the headline description.
An accumulating fund reinvests dividends inside the fund. A distributing fund pays them out to you as cash.

The choice does not change the fund's total return. It changes whether you receive cash you must then decide what to do with, and in many countries it changes when and how the income is taxed. Many funds offer both versions of the same portfolio, distinguished only by a letter in the name.
A fund lending the shares it holds to other market participants in exchange for a fee, while holding collateral against the loan.

Securities lending income can offset a fund's costs, which sounds purely good. It introduces a counterparty relationship the fund did not otherwise have, and the borrower is frequently a short seller. The relevant questions are what proportion of the fund can be lent, how much of the fee is returned to investors rather than kept by the manager, and what collateral is held. All three are in the documentation and none are in the advertisement.

blocks.text: What to look for on any fund fact sheet, in the order that matters. The ongoing charge, from Lesson 7. The fund size, since very small funds are more likely to be closed and merged. The tracking difference over the last three years, not just the fee. Whether replication is physical or synthetic. Whether it accumulates or distributes. And the average spread on the exchange where you would buy it, which is a cost the fact sheet often omits entirely.

Two funds track the same index. The first charges 0.07% and lagged the index by 0.19% a year. The second charges 0.12% and lagged by 0.10%. The second is more expensive on the page and cheaper in reality, and only the tracking difference reveals it.

Pick one broad index ETF and find four numbers in its official documentation: the ongoing charge, the fund size, the tracking difference over three years, and whether it is physical or synthetic. If you cannot find any of the four within ten minutes, that is itself informative — the documents you cannot navigate are the ones you should not buy.
One timing detail affects the price you get and is invisible unless you know to look for it.

A fund holding assets that trade on other exchanges can only be priced accurately while those exchanges are open. A European fund holding Asian companies is trading, during the European afternoon, on a best estimate of what those companies are worth, because their market closed hours earlier. The estimate is usually good and the spread widens to reflect the uncertainty.

The practical consequence is to avoid trading a fund during the periods when its underlying market is shut, and to avoid the first and last minutes of any session. Both are moments when the mechanism that keeps the price near its net asset value is working with less information, and you pay for that in the spread.

quiz.question: An ETF is trading at 50.30 while the basket of shares it holds is worth 50.00 per ETF share. What normally happens next?
options: Nothing — the ETF price is set independently by supply and demand
An authorised participant buys the underlying basket, exchanges it for new ETF shares and sells them, which pushes the two prices together
The fund manager manually resets the ETF price to 50.00
The exchange halts trading until the prices match
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The creation and redemption mechanism turns the gap into an arbitrage opportunity, and pursuing it adds ETF supply and underlying demand until the gap closes. Nobody sets the price by decree — the profit motive does the work. Note that this weakens when the underlying is hard to trade, which is when premiums and discounts widen.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. No one resets the price by hand and trading is not halted. An authorised participant can trade directly with the fund, so a gap between the ETF price and the value of its holdings becomes a profit opportunity — and acting on it is what pushes the two back together.

quiz.question: Fund A charges 0.07% a year and has lagged its index by 0.19% annually. Fund B charges 0.12% and has lagged by 0.10%. Which has served its investors better, and why?
options: Fund A, because its fee is lower
Fund B, because tracking difference measures the total shortfall against the index, and B's is smaller
They are identical, because the fee is what investors pay
Neither, because tracking difference is unrelated to investor returns
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The fee is one input to the shortfall, not the shortfall itself. Trading costs, dividend timing and lending income all contribute. Tracking difference measures the whole gap, and by that measure the more expensive fund delivered more of the index.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. The advertised fee is only part of what separates a fund from its index. Tracking difference captures the total shortfall, and here the fund with the higher fee delivered a smaller one.

quiz.question: What is the main consideration a fund's securities lending programme introduces for its investors?
options: It reduces the fund's return by the amount lent
It creates a counterparty relationship and raises questions about collateral and how much of the fee reaches investors
It prevents the fund from tracking its index
It makes the fund synthetic rather than physical
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Lending generates income that can offset costs, so it is not simply a negative. But it introduces a relationship with a borrower who may fail, and the terms — how much may be lent, what collateral is held, what share of the fee the manager keeps — are in the documentation rather than the marketing.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. Lending generates income rather than reducing returns directly, and it does not change physical replication into synthetic. What it adds is a counterparty, along with questions about collateral and how the fee is split.

lessons.title: Dividends and Total Return
lessons.keyIdea: A dividend is not free money. The share price drops by roughly the payment — what matters is total return, not the yield.

blocks.text: Dividends attract a particular kind of enthusiasm. An income that arrives without selling anything feels like a different category of return from a rising price. Mechanically, it is not.
A cash payment made by a company to its shareholders out of the residual you met in Lesson 1.

The important detail is what happens to the share price when the dividend is paid. The cash leaves the company. A company holding one unit less cash is worth one unit less, and the share price reflects that.
The first day a share trades without the right to the upcoming dividend. Buy on or after this date and the seller keeps the payment.

A share trades at 40.00 and pays a 1.00 dividend. On the ex-dividend date it opens at roughly 39.00. A holder who owned it through that date now has a share worth 39.00 and 1.00 in cash — the same 40.00 they had the day before. Nothing was created.
That word roughly is carrying real weight, and the honest version of this is more interesting than the tidy one.

Elton and Gruber studied this in 1970, in the Review of Economics and Statistics (volume 52, pages 68 to 74), using dividends paid between April 1966 and March 1967. They found the price drop was significantly less than the dividend, on average — and argued the gap reflected tax, since dividends were then taxed more heavily than capital gains, so a dividend was worth less than its face value to the marginal holder.

That explanation is not settled, and the course would be misleading you to present it as though it were. More than a hundred papers have since argued about whether the shortfall is really about tax at all, or about market microstructure — the fact that prices historically moved in discrete tick sizes, so the drop could not land exactly on the dividend. The finding that the drop is less than the dividend is robust. Why has been contested for over fifty years.
The deeper question is whether a company paying dividends is better for you than one that does not.

Miller and Modigliani addressed this in 1961, in the Journal of Business (volume 34, pages 411 to 433). Under a set of idealised assumptions — no taxes, no transaction costs, and investment decisions held fixed — they showed that dividend policy does not affect the value of the firm. A shareholder wanting cash can sell a small part of their holding, and one not wanting cash can reinvest the dividend. The two are equivalent.

The assumptions are obviously not the real world, and that is the point of the result rather than a flaw in it. It tells you where to look. If dividend policy matters in practice, it must matter because of one of the things the model assumed away: tax, costs, or what the payment reveals about management's intentions. It is not because cash paid out is inherently superior to value retained.
The return from price change and dividends together, with dividends assumed reinvested. Price return counts only the price change.

This is the number that actually describes what happened to your money, and it is why comparing two shares on dividend yield alone is a mistake. A high yield can mean a generous payment. It can equally mean a falling price, since yield is the dividend divided by the price — the denominator shrinking raises the yield just as reliably as the numerator growing.

A yield that rises sharply without the dividend changing is a price signal, not an income opportunity. It usually means the market expects the payment to be cut. Screening for the highest yields, without asking why they are high, systematically selects for exactly the companies about to reduce them.

Two shares each yield 5%. One pays 2.50 on a 50.00 price after years of steady increases. The other paid 2.50 on a price that has fallen from 100.00 to 50.00 in eighteen months. The yield is identical and the situations have nothing in common. Only looking at the yield makes them look like the same investment.

None of this makes dividend-paying shares bad, and dividend-focused funds are a legitimate holding. The point is narrower: judge a holding on total return and on why the company pays what it pays. Treat the yield as one input, not as the answer.
If a dividend is not free money, the useful question becomes whether the company can keep paying it.
The proportion of a company's earnings paid out as dividends. A ratio above 100% means the company is paying out more than it earned.

A payout ratio comfortably below 100% means the payment is covered by what the business earns and has room to survive a bad year. A ratio persistently above it means the dividend is being funded from cash reserves, from borrowing, or from selling assets. None of those can continue indefinitely, and the market usually works this out before the announcement.

A company earns 3.00 a share and pays 1.20. The payout ratio is 40%, and earnings could fall by more than half before the dividend was uncovered. Another earns 1.00 and pays 1.30. The ratio is 130%, the shortfall is being funded from somewhere else, and the yield on the screen is describing a payment rather than a promise.
There is also a second way companies return cash, and comparing only dividends misses it entirely.
A company using cash to buy its own shares in the market and cancel them, leaving each remaining share entitled to a larger slice of the same business.

A buyback and a dividend both return cash to owners. The dividend arrives as money you can see. The buyback arrives as a larger ownership proportion, which you cannot see and which shows up only in per-share figures later. A company returning a great deal through buybacks can appear stingy on any dividend screen.

This is why screening for high dividend yield is a weak filter. It excludes companies returning cash a different way, and it selects for companies whose price has fallen, since yield rises when price falls. A screen built on yield alone is partly a screen for recent disappointment.

blocks.text: What to look for on any income-focused holding. The payout ratio and whether it is covered by cash flow rather than only by accounting earnings. Whether the dividend has been cut before, and when. Whether the company also buys back shares. And whether the fund or share is being sold to you on yield alone, which the previous paragraph explains is a filter with a bias built into it.

Take any share with a yield above 6%. Find its payout ratio and its dividend history over the last five years. Then write one sentence explaining why the market is pricing that yield so high. If the honest sentence is that the market expects the payment to be cut, you have learned what the yield was actually telling you.

quiz.question: A share you own at 60.00 pays a 2.00 dividend. On the ex-dividend date the price opens near 58.00. What has happened to your wealth?
options: It has fallen by 2.00 — the price dropped and the dividend does not compensate
It is roughly unchanged — you hold a share worth 58.00 plus 2.00 in cash
It has risen by 2.00 — the dividend is income on top of the share
It depends entirely on whether you reinvest the dividend
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The cash left the company, so the share is worth that much less, and you hold the cash instead. Roughly is the right word — the measured drop is reliably a little less than the dividend, and why that is has been argued about since Elton and Gruber in 1970. But the headline point stands: a dividend moves value from one pocket to another rather than creating it.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. The dividend is paid out of the company, so the company — and therefore the share — is worth less by about that amount. You have not gained 2.00 or lost 2.00; you now hold a share worth about 58.00 plus 2.00 in cash. This is why total return, not yield, is the number that describes what happened.

quiz.question: A company earns 1.00 a share and pays a dividend of 1.30. What does this tell you?
options: The company is highly profitable and rewarding shareholders
The payout is not covered by earnings and is being funded from reserves, borrowing or asset sales, which cannot continue indefinitely
The dividend will certainly rise next year
The share is undervalued relative to its income
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. A payout ratio of 130% means the company is distributing more than it earns. The money has to come from somewhere else, and none of the available sources are permanent. The market usually anticipates the cut before it is announced.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. Paying out more than you earn is not a sign of strength. The shortfall must be funded from cash reserves, borrowing or asset sales, and each of those has a limit — which is why a very high yield is often a forecast of a cut.

quiz.question: Why does screening for high dividend yield alone select a biased sample of companies?
options: Because high-yield companies are always more profitable
Because yield rises when price falls, so the screen partly selects for recent disappointment, and it excludes companies returning cash through buybacks instead
Because dividend yields are not publicly reported
Because high-yield shares cannot be held in funds
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Yield is the dividend divided by the price, so a falling price raises it mechanically. The screen therefore over-represents companies the market has marked down, and it misses companies returning large amounts of cash through buybacks, which show up in per-share figures rather than in yield.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. The bias comes from the arithmetic of the ratio. A falling price raises yield without any improvement in the business, and companies returning cash through buybacks are invisible to a yield screen entirely.

keyTerms.def: A cash payment from a company to its shareholders.
The first day a share trades without the right to the upcoming dividend.
Price change plus dividends reinvested — what actually happened to your money.
The dividend divided by the share price. Rises when the price falls, which is often why it is high.

lessons.title: What It Costs to Own
lessons.keyIdea: A fee is charged on the whole balance every year, so it compounds against you. 1.45% a year became a third of the final pot.

blocks.text: Fees are quoted as small annual percentages, which makes them sound trivial. The arithmetic of compounding them over an investing lifetime is not trivial at all, and it is the most reliably ignored number in personal investing.
The annual fee a fund charges, as a percentage of the money you have invested with it. It is deducted from the fund's assets, so you never see a bill.

That last part matters more than it should. A fee you are invoiced for gets noticed and questioned. A fee deducted quietly from the fund's value simply shows up as slightly worse performance, which is easy to attribute to markets rather than to costs.
Here is what the difference actually does. The figures below assume 10,000 invested for 30 years with an underlying return of 7% a year, and they are computed rather than estimated.

With no fee at all, 10,000 becomes about 76,123. At an expense ratio of 0.05%, typical of a broad index ETF, it becomes about 75,063. At 0.75% it becomes about 61,641. At 1.50%, a level not unusual for an actively managed fund plus an adviser, it becomes about 49,840.

Compare the two ends. The difference in fee is 1.45% a year. The difference in outcome is about 25,223 — the expensive option finishes with roughly 66% of what the cheap one produced. A 1.45% annual charge consumed about a third of the final pot.

The reason the effect is so much larger than the headline number is that the fee is charged on the whole balance every year, including on the gains that previous years' fees have already reduced. Compounding works on costs exactly as it works on returns, and in the same direction — away from you.

The same effect on a contribution schedule: 200 a month for 30 years at 7% gross is 72,000 of your own money paid in. At 0.05% it grows to about 241,601. At 1.50% it grows to about 182,722. The 58,879 difference is close to what you contributed over the first twenty-four years.

A fee is one of the few things about investing you can control completely, and it is certain. The return is uncertain, the timing is uncertain, your own behaviour is uncertain. The expense ratio is a known number you can read before you buy and change by choosing a different fund. Spending effort on the certain, controllable input before the uncertain, uncontrollable one is simply the better use of attention.

There is a structural argument here too, and it is unusually clean. William Sharpe set it out in 1991 in the Financial Analysts Journal (volume 47, issue 1, pages 7 to 9), in a paper called The Arithmetic of Active Management.

The argument is arithmetic, not empirical, which is what makes it strong. All the shares in a market are held by someone. The passively managed money holds the market in proportion, so it earns the market return before costs. The remaining money is actively managed and, taken together, must therefore also hold the rest of the market in proportion — so it too earns the market return before costs. Active management as a whole cannot beat the market before costs, because in aggregate it is the market. After costs, and active costs are higher, it must on average do worse.

Read what that claim is and is not. It does not say no active manager can beat the market — plainly some do. It says the average actively managed unit of currency must underperform the average passive one after costs, as a matter of arithmetic rather than evidence. Individual skill is a claim about the distribution around that average, not a repeal of it.

The expense ratio is also not the whole cost. Lesson 3 covered the spread you pay each time you trade. Funds pay spreads too, inside the fund, when they buy and sell — so a fund that trades a lot carries costs beyond its published fee. Taxes are a third layer, and depend on your own circumstances.

Chapter 4 returns to this with the full picture across a lifetime. For now the practical instruction is small: before buying any fund, find the expense ratio, and compare it to the alternatives that hold roughly the same thing. It is a two-minute check with a larger effect on your outcome than almost anything else you will do.
Finding the true figure is harder than it should be, mostly because the same number has several names.
A standardised annual cost figure for a fund, covering management and most operating costs. Also encountered as the total expense ratio, and broadly comparable to the American expense ratio.

These names are not perfectly interchangeable and the small print differs by jurisdiction, but they answer the same question: what proportion of your holding is deducted each year. What none of them include is the cost of the fund's own trading, or the spread you pay on the exchange, or any platform fee charged by whoever holds the account.

The advertised fee is a floor, not a total. A fund at 0.20% held on a platform charging 0.35% costs 0.55% a year before you count spreads. Chapter 4 does the full arithmetic on that stack, and the result is larger than most people expect.
One qualification to the general rule that cheaper is better, because the previous lesson's finding cuts both ways.

The fee is what you are charged. The tracking difference is what you actually lost against the index, and it includes the fee plus everything else. Choosing purely on the advertised number can occasionally pick the fund that delivered less of the index. The correct comparison is the shortfall over several years, and the fee is the best single predictor of it rather than a substitute for it.

blocks.text: What to look for before buying any fund. The ongoing charge in the official document rather than a comparison website. The platform or custody fee, which is charged separately and often quietly. The tracking difference over three years. And the total of all recurring charges written on one line, because no provider will ever present that total for you.

A reader compares two broad index funds and finds 0.07% and 0.22%. The difference looks negligible. On 200 a month for 30 years at 7% gross, it is roughly 6,000 of final value — for a choice that takes ten minutes and requires no forecast about anything.

Write down every recurring percentage you currently pay: fund charges, platform fees, and any advice fee. Add them into a single number. Then find the cheapest equivalent broad fund available to you and write its total next to yours. The gap between those two figures is the one number in this course you can change today with certainty.

quiz.question: Two funds hold nearly identical assets. One charges 0.05% a year, the other 1.50%. Over 30 years at a 7% underlying return, roughly what happens?
options: The expensive fund ends up about 1.45% behind, matching the fee difference
The expensive fund ends up with about two thirds of what the cheap fund produced
The difference is negligible, because 1.45% a year is a small number
The expensive fund catches up, because higher fees usually buy better management
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. On 10,000 over 30 years the cheap fund produces about 75,063 and the expensive one about 49,840 — roughly 66% of it. The fee is charged on the entire balance every year, so it compounds, which is why a 1.45% annual difference turns into about a third of the final pot rather than 1.45% of it.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. The fee applies to your whole balance every year, not once, so it compounds against you. On 10,000 over 30 years at 7%, the difference between 0.05% and 1.50% is about 25,223 — the expensive fund finishes with roughly two thirds of what the cheap one produced.

quiz.question: A fund advertises an ongoing charge of 0.20% and is held on a platform charging 0.35% a year. What is the recurring cost of the position?
options: 0.20%, since the fund charge is what matters
0.35%, since the platform charge replaces the fund charge
At least 0.55%, because recurring charges stack and neither figure includes trading spreads
0.15%, the difference between the two
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Recurring charges add together, and the advertised fund fee is a floor rather than a total. Neither figure includes the fund's own trading costs or the spread you pay on the exchange, so 0.55% is the minimum rather than the answer.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. The two charges are levied by different parties and both apply, so they add: 0.55% before any trading costs. This is why the only useful figure is the total of every recurring charge written on one line.

quiz.question: Why is the advertised fee not always sufficient to choose between two funds tracking the same index?
options: Because fees change every month
Because the tracking difference measures the total shortfall against the index, and a fund with a slightly higher fee can deliver more of the index
Because fees are not disclosed for index funds
Because index funds do not charge fees at all
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The fee is one component of the shortfall; trading costs, dividend handling and lending income are others. The fee remains the best single predictor of the total, but the total itself is the tracking difference, and that is what to compare over several years.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. Fees are disclosed and reasonably stable. The point is that the fee is only part of what separates a fund from its index — the full gap is the tracking difference, and occasionally the cheaper-looking fund delivers less of the index.

keyTerms.def: A fund's annual fee as a percentage of assets, deducted from the fund rather than billed.
Selecting holdings in an attempt to beat an index, rather than tracking it.
Holding the market in proportion, tracking an index rather than trying to beat it.

lessons.chapterTitle: Reading a Company and a Market
lessons.title: Reading the Three Statements
lessons.keyIdea: Profit is an opinion shaped by accounting choices. Cash is a fact. That is why the three statements exist rather than one.

blocks.text: A company reports three financial statements, and beginners usually read one of them. Reading all three is what separates a view of a business from a view of a headline.
Each answers a different question, and none answers the others.
What the company earned and spent over a period. It answers: was the business profitable during these months?
What the company owns and owes at a single moment. It answers: what does the business consist of right now?
Where cash actually came from and went over a period. It answers: did money genuinely move?
The distinction that matters most is between the first and the third, and it comes down to timing.

Revenue is recorded when it is earned, not when it is paid. A company that delivers goods in March and is paid in July records the sale in March. That is not a trick — it describes the business more faithfully than waiting for the cheque. But it opens a gap between reported profit and money in the bank.

A company reports 10 million of profit for the year. Its cash flow statement shows cash from operations of 2 million. The difference sits in receivables — sales made but not yet collected. Both numbers are accurate. Together they say something neither says alone: the business is selling, and it is not yet being paid.

Neither figure is the truth on its own. What you are looking for is whether they move together over time. Profit rising while operating cash flow stagnates, year after year, is the pattern worth understanding rather than dismissing.

Profit involves judgement in a way cash does not. How quickly to depreciate equipment, when a sale counts as made, how much to set aside for bad debts — each is a legitimate choice within the rules, and each moves reported profit. Cash from operations is harder to shape because it tracks money that actually arrived. This is why experienced readers start with the cash flow statement, which is the opposite of what most beginners do.
The balance sheet answers a different question again: not how the year went, but what the company is made of.

It always balances, because of an identity rather than a coincidence. Everything the company owns was funded either by borrowing or by owners. Assets equal liabilities plus equity — and that equity line is the residual claim from Lesson 1, in accounting form.

A company holds 500 million of assets and owes 400 million. Equity is 100 million. If the assets turn out to be worth 380 million — a factory worth less than its book value, stock that will not sell — the liabilities do not shrink. Equity absorbs all of it and goes negative. The shareholders were wiped out while the lenders were merely worried.

That example is Lesson 1 again from another angle, and it is why the balance sheet matters even to someone who never intends to value a company. It tells you how much has to go wrong before the residual is gone.

One practical habit is worth more than any ratio. Read the same three statements for the same company across three or four years, side by side, rather than one year in isolation. A single year tells you almost nothing; a trend across several tells you what direction the business is moving and whether the profit and the cash agree.

Everything in the next lesson — every valuation multiple — is built from these numbers. A multiple calculated on a profit figure you have not examined is a precise-looking number resting on an unexamined one.
One figure drawn from the cash flow statement is worth more than most ratios, because it answers the question an owner actually has.
Cash generated by operations, less the spending needed to maintain and expand the company's assets. Roughly, the cash genuinely available to the owners.

Operating cash flow tells you the business produced cash. Free cash flow tells you how much survived the cost of keeping the business running. A company generating strong operating cash that spends all of it replacing worn-out equipment is not producing anything for its owners, however healthy the top of the statement looks.

Cash from operations is 120 million. Capital spending is 110 million. Free cash flow is 10 million. The same company reports 90 million of profit. The profit figure describes a business four times more generous to its owners than the cash figure does, and only one of the two can be spent.
The gap between profit and cash usually has a specific location, and it is normally worth finding.
Money owed to the company by customers who have been billed but have not yet paid.

Receivables growing considerably faster than revenue is one of the oldest warning signs in company analysis. It can be ordinary growth in a business that bills before it collects. It can also mean the company is booking sales to customers who will not pay, or offering unusually generous terms to keep revenue rising. The statements will not tell you which, but they will tell you to ask.

blocks.caption: Profit is an opinion shaped by accounting choices. Cash is a fact. That is why there are three statements.
