blocks.text: What to look for when you read a set of accounts. Compare profit with operating cash flow across at least three years and note whether the gap is stable or widening. Check whether free cash flow is positive after capital spending. Look at how fast receivables and inventory are growing relative to revenue. And read the notes to the accounts, which is where anything genuinely awkward is disclosed in the smallest available typeface.

Choose any listed company and open its last three annual reports. Write down six numbers: profit and operating cash flow for each year. Then write one sentence saying whether they moved together. That comparison, done honestly, filters out more bad holdings than any valuation ratio you will learn next lesson.
A fourth number sits across all three statements and changes what every per-share figure means.
The number of shares the company has issued. Earnings per share, book value per share and dividends per share are all divided by it.

A company can increase its total profit while its profit per share falls, if it issued more shares along the way. It can also raise profit per share without the business improving at all, by buying shares back. Neither is dishonest, and both change the number most people quote without changing the business behind it.

Total profit rises from 100 million to 110 million, a 10% improvement. Over the same period the share count rises from 50 million to 60 million to fund an acquisition. Earnings per share fall from 2.00 to about 1.83. The company grew and each owner's slice shrank.

quiz.question: A company reports growing profits for three years, while cash from operations stays flat. What is the most reasonable reading?
options: The profits are fraudulent
Nothing — profit and cash flow are unrelated measures
Something is worth investigating: profit involves judgement, cash does not, and a persistent gap has a cause worth finding
The company should be valued on profit, since it is the more complete figure
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The gap is not proof of anything by itself — it can be rapid growth funded by extending credit to customers, which is normal. But profit reflects accounting judgement and cash reflects money that moved, so a persistent divergence has a cause, and finding it is the work.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. It is not evidence of fraud, and the two figures are certainly related. The point is that profit involves legitimate judgement — depreciation, when a sale counts, provisions — while cash from operations tracks money that actually arrived. A gap that persists for years is a question to investigate, not a verdict either way.

quiz.question: A company reports 90 million of profit, 120 million of cash from operations and 110 million of capital spending. What is the most useful reading for an owner?
options: The business is highly profitable, since profit and operating cash flow are both strong
Free cash flow is about 10 million, so very little of the reported profit is genuinely available to owners
The company is in distress, because capital spending exceeds profit
Profit is understated and should be adjusted upward
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Operating cash flow of 120 million less capital spending of 110 million leaves roughly 10 million of free cash flow. The 90 million profit figure describes a far more generous business than the cash actually available, and only the cash can be paid out or reinvested by choice.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. High capital spending is normal in many industries and is not by itself distress. What matters is what remains: 120 million in, 110 million out, leaves about 10 million of free cash flow against a reported profit of 90 million.

quiz.question: A company's receivables are growing much faster than its revenue. What does this justify?
options: Immediately concluding the accounts are fraudulent
Concluding the company is more profitable than reported
Asking why — it can be ordinary growth in a business that bills before collecting, or sales booked to customers who may not pay
Nothing, since receivables are not part of the financial statements
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The pattern is a question rather than a verdict. It is consistent with healthy growth and with revenue being recognised on sales that will not be collected, and the statements alone cannot distinguish them. The value of noticing it is that it tells you where to look.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. Fast-growing receivables are a well-known warning sign, but they are not proof of anything on their own — many growing businesses bill well before they collect. The correct response is to investigate, not to conclude.

keyTerms.def: What was earned and spent over a period.
What the company owns and owes at one moment. Assets = liabilities + equity.
Where cash actually came from and went.

lessons.title: Valuation Multiples and Their Assumptions
lessons.keyIdea: A multiple is a forecast compressed into one number. A low one is a question about why, not an answer about value.

blocks.text: Every valuation multiple is a ratio of what you pay to something you get. They are useful, quick, and routinely misread, because a multiple looks like a measurement when it is actually a summary of expectations.
The share price divided by earnings per share. Roughly, how many years of current earnings you are paying for one share.
A share costs 40.00 and the company earned 2.00 per share last year. The P/E is 20. At that earnings level, twenty years of profit would equal what you paid.

The phrase at that earnings level is where the whole difficulty lives. Nobody buys a company expecting earnings to stay exactly where they are. The P/E is therefore not a measure of value; it is a measure of what the market expects, expressed through a number about the past.

This makes a low P/E genuinely ambiguous. It can mean the market is wrong and the shares are cheap. It can equally mean the market expects earnings to fall, and the ratio is low because the denominator is about to shrink.

Two companies both trade at a P/E of 7. One is a stable business the market has overlooked. The other is losing its largest customer next year, and everyone knows it. The ratio is identical. One is a bargain and one is arithmetic catching up with reality, and the ratio alone cannot tell you which.

Screening for the lowest P/E ratios and buying them systematically selects for companies whose earnings the market expects to fall. Sometimes the market is wrong, which is the entire basis of value investing. But the screen is not finding cheap companies — it is finding disliked ones, and sorting those two apart is the actual work.
A second multiple compares price to what the company owns rather than what it earns.
The share price divided by the balance-sheet equity per share — what you pay against the accounting value of the residual.

P/B travels better than P/E for companies with real physical assets, and badly for companies whose value is mostly people, software or brands. A firm whose main assets are its employees can be extremely valuable and carry almost nothing on its balance sheet, which produces a P/B that means very little.
Company value including debt, divided by earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. Used to compare businesses with different levels of borrowing.

This exists because P/E is affected by how a company is financed. Two identical businesses, one funded by debt and one by equity, can show very different P/E ratios for reasons that have nothing to do with the operations. Enterprise value looks past the financing to the business underneath.

EBITDA deliberately excludes depreciation, and depreciation is the accounting acknowledgement that equipment wears out and must be replaced. For a business that genuinely consumes physical assets, excluding it flatters the picture. It is a useful comparison tool and a poor summary of what a company keeps.

The one rule that holds across all of them: a multiple is only meaningful against a comparison. Twenty is not high or low. It is high against a stable utility and low against a fast-growing software company, and comparing across those two tells you almost nothing.

Compare like with like, over several years, and treat every unusual number as a question rather than a signal. The next lesson asks whether systematically buying the cheap-looking ones has actually worked.
One distinction changes what a P/E means before you interpret it at all.
A trailing P/E uses earnings already reported. A forward P/E uses analysts' estimates of earnings not yet earned.

A trailing multiple is a fact divided by a fact. A forward multiple contains a forecast, and the forecast was made by people whose estimates are revised regularly and are more optimistic than accurate on average. A company can look expensive on trailing earnings and cheap on forward earnings purely because someone expects a good year.

When a share is described as cheap, ask which earnings figure is in the denominator and who produced it. A forward P/E of 11 is not a price; it is a price divided by a hope. If the estimate falls, the multiple rises without the share moving at all.
There is a second trap that catches careful people, and it runs in the opposite direction to intuition.
A company whose earnings rise and fall sharply with the economic cycle — miners, carmakers, chemicals, shipping and similar.

For a cyclical company the multiple is most misleading exactly when it looks most attractive. At the top of a cycle, earnings are at their highest, so the P/E is at its lowest, and the shares look cheap immediately before earnings collapse. At the bottom, earnings are minimal and the P/E is enormous or undefined, which is often the better moment to buy.

A mining company earns 5.00 a share at the peak of a commodity cycle, and trades at 30.00 — a P/E of 6. Two years later the commodity price has halved, the company earns 0.50, and the shares trade at 20.00 — a P/E of 40. The low multiple marked the danger and the high one marked the opportunity, which is the reverse of the screening rule.

blocks.caption: For a cyclical company the multiple looks most attractive at exactly the wrong moment.

blocks.text: What to look for whenever you use a multiple. Establish whether the earnings are trailing or forecast. Compare against the company's own history over several years, not only against its industry today. Ask whether the business is cyclical, and if so where in the cycle those earnings sit. And treat any multiple far from its peers as the beginning of an investigation rather than the end of one.

Take one company and find its P/E in each of the last five years, along with its earnings per share in each of those years. Write down which changed more: the multiple or the earnings. The answer tells you whether the market has been repricing the same business, or repricing a business that was genuinely changing.
One more caution about comparison, because it is the step where multiples are most often misused.

Multiples do not travel well across industries or across countries. A software company and a shipping company have different capital requirements, different growth prospects and different risks, so their multiples should differ permanently rather than converge. Accounting standards also differ by jurisdiction, which means the earnings figure in the denominator is not always constructed the same way.

A cross-border or cross-industry comparison showing one market or sector as cheap is usually measuring a structural difference rather than an opportunity. The comparison that carries information is a company against its own history and against direct competitors doing the same thing in the same place.

quiz.question: A company trades at a P/E of 6 while its industry averages 15. What does this tell you?
options: The shares are cheap and should be bought
The shares are expensive relative to peers
That the market expects something different about this company — and finding out what is the actual work
Nothing at all; P/E ratios are meaningless
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. A P/E well below peers is a question, not an answer. It usually means the market expects earnings to fall. Sometimes that expectation is wrong, which is where returns come from — but the ratio alone cannot distinguish an overlooked business from one whose problems are already known.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. A low P/E is not automatically cheap: the ratio uses past earnings, so it falls when the market expects future earnings to drop. It is a prompt to investigate why the market disagrees with the historical figure, not a verdict in either direction.

quiz.question: A cyclical mining company trades at a P/E of 6 at the peak of a commodity cycle and a P/E of 40 two years later. What does this pattern illustrate?
options: That the shares became more expensive as the business improved
That for cyclical companies the multiple looks most attractive when earnings are at their peak and about to fall — the reverse of the screening rule
That P/E ratios are meaningless for all companies
That the company changed its accounting method
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Peak earnings in the denominator produce a low multiple precisely when the earnings are least sustainable, and depressed earnings produce a high one at the moment that is often the better entry. For cyclicals, a low P/E is a warning at least as often as it is a bargain.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. Nothing changed about the accounting, and the multiple is not meaningless — it is misleading in a specific, predictable direction for cyclical businesses. Peak earnings make the multiple look lowest just before they fall.

quiz.question: Why does a forward P/E require more care than a trailing one?
options: Because forward P/E ratios are not published
Because it divides price by an estimate rather than a reported figure, so the multiple can rise on a downgrade without the share moving
Because forward earnings are always higher than trailing earnings
Because trailing P/E ratios ignore the share price
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. A trailing multiple divides one fact by another. A forward multiple contains a forecast made by people whose estimates are revised regularly, so a cheap-looking forward multiple can become an ordinary one on an estimate cut alone — with no change in the share price.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. Forward multiples are widely published and are not automatically higher or lower. The care they require comes from the denominator being an estimate, which can be revised down and take the apparent cheapness with it.

lessons.chapterTitle: Reading a Company and a Market
lessons.title: Growth, Value and the Factor Evidence
lessons.keyIdea: Cheap-looking shares beat expensive ones for decades in the data. Then they did not, for a long time. Both facts are the lesson.

blocks.text: The previous lesson left a question open: does systematically buying the cheap-looking companies actually work? It is one of the most studied questions in finance, and the honest answer has two halves that point in different directions.
Buying shares that look cheap against a fundamental measure such as book value or earnings, on the expectation that the market has been too pessimistic.
Buying shares that look expensive against those measures, on the expectation that the underlying business will grow into and past the price.

The landmark study is Fama and French, in the Journal of Finance in 1992 (volume 47, issue 2, pages 427 to 465). They examined which characteristics actually explained differences in average share returns, and found that two easily measured variables did most of the work: company size, and book-to-market equity — the accounting value of a company against its market price.

High book-to-market means the market price is low relative to the accounting value. Those shares, in their data, earned higher average returns. That finding became known as the value premium, and it reshaped the field.

What is easy to miss is what the finding is not. It is a statement about averages across large baskets of shares over long periods. It is not a statement that cheap shares outperform reliably, and certainly not that any particular cheap share will.

A premium that shows up as an average over decades can be absent for years at a time, and the value premium has spent long stretches doing exactly that. An investor who adopted the strategy on the strength of the historical average and then lived through one of those stretches experienced something the average never described. The average is real. It is also not what any individual investor gets.
Two explanations compete, and they have never been fully reconciled.

The risk explanation says cheap companies are cheap because they are genuinely riskier — more likely to be in distress, more vulnerable in a downturn — and the extra return is payment for bearing that. On this reading the premium is not a free lunch and should persist, because the risk does.

The behavioural explanation says investors over-extrapolate: they assume struggling companies will keep struggling and glamorous ones will keep growing, pushing prices too far in both directions. On this reading the premium is a mistake — and mistakes that become widely known tend to shrink.

The two explanations make different predictions about what happens after a finding is published and becomes famous. If value pays for risk, publishing changes nothing. If value is a behavioural error, publishing should reduce it as money flows in to exploit it. Decades on, the argument about which happened is still live.

Be careful with any strategy discovered by searching historical data. Test enough rules against the same history and some will look excellent by chance alone. The course made this point in Foundations Chapter 3 about chart patterns, and it applies with equal force here — the difference is that the value premium was found in a much larger body of data and has been re-tested across many markets, which is a reason to take it more seriously, not a reason to treat it as settled.

What should a reader do with this? Not much, directly — and that is the point. The practical value is not a strategy. It is calibration: an effect real enough to reshape academic finance still spent years failing to appear. Any claim that some rule reliably beats the market should be measured against that.
A further complication sits between the published finding and anything you could actually hold: the definition itself is a choice.

Fama and French measured cheapness as book-to-market — the accounting value of the company against its market price. Other researchers and funds use earnings, cash flow, sales or dividends. These produce overlapping but genuinely different sets of companies, and they have not performed identically. A finding about one definition of value is not automatically a finding about the fund that calls itself a value fund.

Book value has also become a weaker measure of what a company is over the period since the original study. Accounting rules treat a factory as an asset and much research, software development and brand building as an expense. A company whose main assets are people and code can show very little book value while being extremely valuable, which distorts the measure rather than the companies.
Then there is the gap between a documented premium and a realised return.
The trading costs, spreads, taxes and fees incurred in actually holding a strategy, which are absent from the paper describing it.

A published premium is measured on paper portfolios, rebalanced without cost. A fund reproducing it pays spreads on every trade, a management fee every year, and tax where it applies. A premium of two percentage points on paper can be most of the way to nothing after the costs of capturing it, and Chapter 1 Lesson 7 showed how quickly annual charges compound.

blocks.text: What to look for whenever a strategy is presented with historical evidence. Ask how cheapness or quality or momentum was defined, and whether the fund uses the same definition as the study. Ask over what period the result held, and whether the period included a long stretch where it did not work. Ask what it cost to implement. And ask what has happened since the finding was published, because a strategy known to everyone is a different proposition from one nobody had noticed.

Find any fund that describes itself as a value fund and locate the measure it actually uses to select companies. Then find its performance against a plain broad index over the last ten years. Whatever the result, you now know something more useful than the premium itself: whether this particular implementation delivered it.
It is worth separating two things this literature is used to justify, because only one of them follows from it.
Holding a broad, diversified fund constructed to lean toward a characteristic such as value, size or momentum, rather than selecting individual companies.

The evidence concerns large baskets held over long periods. It supports the idea of a tilt, applied across hundreds of companies with an intended holding period measured in decades. It says nothing whatever about buying six cheap-looking companies, which is a different activity that borrows the research as decoration.

If you adopt a tilt, the commitment has to outlast the drought. A value tilt abandoned after five poor years captures the underperformance and none of the premium, which is a worse outcome than never tilting at all. That is a behavioural requirement rather than an analytical one, and it is the part most people fail.

quiz.question: Fama and French found that high book-to-market shares earned higher average returns. What does that entitle an investor to conclude?
options: Cheap shares reliably beat expensive ones, so buying them is close to free money
That across large baskets over long periods there was a premium — which can be, and has been, absent for years at a time
The finding has been disproved and value investing does not work
Individual cheap shares will outperform individual expensive ones
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. It is an average across large baskets over long periods, and averages of that kind conceal long stretches that look nothing like them. Whether the premium is payment for risk or a behavioural error is still argued, and the two explanations disagree about whether it should survive being famous.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. The finding is real and important, but it describes averages across large baskets over decades — not reliability, and certainly not individual shares. The value premium has gone missing for years at a stretch, which is exactly why "it worked on average historically" is a weaker claim than it sounds.

quiz.question: Two funds both call themselves value funds. Why might their holdings and returns differ substantially?
options: Because one of them must be mislabelled
Because cheapness can be defined by book value, earnings, cash flow, sales or dividends, and these select overlapping but genuinely different companies
Because value investing only works in some countries
Because one fund uses forward estimates and the other is not permitted to
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Fama and French measured book-to-market, but the word value covers several different measures that pick different companies and have not performed identically. A published finding about one definition is not automatically a finding about a fund using another.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. Neither fund need be mislabelled. Value has no single definition — book value, earnings, cash flow, sales and dividends are all used — and the choice materially changes which companies are selected.

quiz.question: Why can a documented premium of two percentage points a year be close to nothing for an investor who tries to capture it?
options: Because published premia are usually fabricated
Because implementation costs — spreads, management fees and taxes — apply to a real fund but not to the paper portfolios the study measured
Because premia only apply to institutional investors
Because the premium is measured after all costs by convention
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Academic portfolios are rebalanced without cost. A real fund pays spreads on every trade, an annual fee, and tax where it applies. Those costs are subtracted from the premium rather than from some separate budget, and Chapter 1 Lesson 7 showed how an annual charge compounds.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. The studies are not fabricated and the premia are generally reported before implementation costs, not after. The gap between paper and portfolio is spreads, fees and taxes — all of which come out of the premium itself.

lessons.chapterTitle: Reading a Company and a Market
lessons.title: Market Efficiency — and What It Means for You
lessons.keyIdea: A perfectly efficient market cannot exist, because nobody would be paid to make it efficient. The useful question is how hard it is to beat, not whether it is possible.

blocks.text: Behind every question in this chapter sits a bigger one: how much is already in the price? If a company's problems are known, they are priced. If they are priced, knowing them is not an edge.
The idea that share prices already reflect available information, so that information cannot be used to earn better-than-average returns.
The idea is usually split into three strengths, which is more useful than treating it as one claim.

The weak form says past prices are already reflected, so studying price history alone cannot produce an edge. The semi-strong form says all public information is reflected, so reading published accounts and news cannot either. The strong form says even private information is reflected — a claim almost nobody defends, and one that insider-trading law implicitly rejects.

A company announces disappointing results at 07:00. By the time the market opens the price has already moved. An investor who reads the announcement at 09:00 and sells is not acting on information — they are acting after the price has absorbed it. The information was public for two hours, which in this context is a long time.
The most useful contribution to this debate is an argument that the strong version cannot be true at all, and it is a matter of logic rather than data.

Grossman and Stiglitz published it in the American Economic Review in 1980 (volume 70, issue 3, pages 393 to 408), under the title On the Impossibility of Informationally Efficient Markets. The argument runs: gathering information costs money. People gather it because doing so is profitable. But it is only profitable if prices do not already reflect it. So if prices perfectly reflected all information, nobody would have any reason to gather it — and prices would stop reflecting it.
A perfectly efficient market therefore destroys the activity that makes it efficient. Some inefficiency has to persist, as the payment that keeps analysts analysing.

This is not a licence to assume you are the one collecting that payment. The argument says the reward for information gathering must be positive in aggregate. It says nothing about who receives it, and the professionals doing it full time have better data, faster execution and more time than you do. "Markets are not perfectly efficient" and "I can beat them" are separated by a great deal.

Set the theory against Lesson 7's arithmetic and the practical picture is clear. Sharpe's result says active management in aggregate must underperform after costs. Grossman and Stiglitz say some opportunity must exist for someone. Both are true: there are rewards, they are competed for by well-resourced professionals, and the average participant pays more in costs than they recover.

Consider how an ordinary investor might realistically find an edge. Not by reading published results, which are priced within minutes. Not from price charts, which every participant sees. Possibly from a genuinely long horizon — being willing to hold through a decade that a fund manager judged quarterly cannot survive. That is a structural advantage a private investor actually has, and it does not require beating anyone at analysis.

That is the honest conclusion of this chapter. Efficiency is a spectrum, not a switch. The reachable edge for most readers is not better information but a longer horizon and lower costs — both of which are available without predicting anything.
The Grossman and Stiglitz argument has an application that has become steadily more relevant, and it is worth following to its uncomfortable end.

Index funds do no research. They buy what the rule specifies at whatever price the market currently sets. Their existence depends on that price being roughly right, and the price is made right by the people who do research and trade on it — the people Sharpe's arithmetic says lose to the index in aggregate after costs.

That is the paradox stated in its sharpest form. The rational choice for an individual is to pay nothing and accept the market price. If everyone made that choice, nobody would be setting the price. Nothing in the theory identifies where the tipping point is, and anyone claiming to know precisely how much active management a market needs is guessing.

What this does not license is the conclusion that you should therefore pay for active management. The argument establishes that someone must do the price discovery. It says nothing about whether you can identify in advance which manager will be paid for it, which is a separate and much harder question.
It is also worth separating two claims that get merged.

The first is that prices reflect information. The second is that prices are correct. Efficiency in the technical sense means the first, not the second. A market can absorb every available fact promptly and still be wrong about the future, because the future is not currently available information. The dot-com case study in Chapter 5 is a market that priced known facts efficiently and valued them on a story that did not hold.

blocks.text: What to look for whenever someone offers you an edge. Ask what specifically they know that the market does not, and how they came to know it. Ask why the information has not already moved the price if it is genuinely public. Ask how long they expect the advantage to survive being described to you. And treat any answer of the form the market has not noticed, about a widely followed company, as the least likely explanation available.

Take the next investment recommendation you encounter, from any source. Write down the specific piece of information it rests on, and the date that information became public. If the price already moved on that date, you have watched semi-strong efficiency work — and you have learned what the recommendation was actually worth.
There is one category of genuinely reliable edge, and it is worth naming precisely so that it can be dismissed properly.

Information that is material and not public would reliably beat the market. Trading on it is also illegal in every developed market, and prosecutions are routine. This matters to the argument rather than to your conduct: the one form of information advantage that clearly works is the one the law removes from the available set, which is part of why the remaining edges are so thin.

What is left for a private investor is not an information advantage but a structural one. You have no clients who can withdraw money, no quarterly performance to report, and no career risk from looking wrong for three years. A professional cannot always hold through a long drawdown even when the analysis says to. You can, and that is the only durable advantage most readers will ever have.

quiz.question: What does the Grossman and Stiglitz argument establish?
options: That markets are perfectly efficient, so analysis is pointless
That markets are completely inefficient and easy to beat
That a perfectly efficient market is impossible, because nobody would gather information if prices already reflected it
That only insiders can make money in markets
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct — and note it is a logical argument, not an empirical one. Some inefficiency must survive as the payment that keeps information-gathering worthwhile. It does not follow that you are the one collecting that payment: it is competed for by full-time professionals with better data and faster execution.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. The argument is narrower and cleverer than any of those. It says perfect efficiency is self-defeating: if prices already reflected everything, nobody would pay to gather information, so prices would stop reflecting it. Some inefficiency must persist — which is not the same as saying it is available to you.

quiz.question: Why does the growth of index investing make the Grossman and Stiglitz argument more pointed?
options: Because index funds set prices more accurately than active managers
Because index funds accept the price the market sets, so they depend on the researchers whom Sharpe's arithmetic says lose to the index in aggregate
Because index funds are legally required to conduct research
Because index funds only hold companies that are correctly priced
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Indexing is rational for an individual precisely because someone else is doing the price discovery. The theory does not tell us where the tipping point lies, and nobody claiming to know how much active management a market needs can support the number.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. Index funds do no research at all — they buy what the rule specifies at the prevailing price. That is exactly why their success depends on the activity of the researchers who, in aggregate and after costs, lose to them.

quiz.question: What is the difference between a market that is efficient and a market that is correct?
options: There is none — efficiency means prices are correct
Efficiency means prices reflect available information; being correct about the future is a separate claim, since the future is not available information
Efficiency applies only to bonds, correctness only to shares
A correct market has no volatility
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Efficiency is a claim about the absorption of information, not about foresight. A market can price every known fact promptly and still be badly wrong about what happens next, which is precisely what the dot-com case study in Chapter 5 shows.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. The two are routinely merged and should not be. Efficiency says available information is in the price. It makes no promise that the resulting price will look sensible in hindsight, because the future was never available information.

keyTerms.def: The idea that prices already reflect available information.
Past prices are already reflected in the current price.
All public information is already reflected.

lessons.chapterTitle: Reading a Company and a Market
lessons.title: Diversification Across Sectors and Countries
lessons.keyIdea: Diversification removes the risk specific to one company. It cannot remove the risk common to all of them, and the number of holdings you need is still argued about.

blocks.text: Holding more than one company reduces risk. That much is uncontroversial. How much, how quickly, and how many holdings it takes are all less settled than the usual advice suggests.
Risk attached to one company — a failed product, a fire, a fraud. It can be diversified away, because these events are largely unrelated across companies.
Risk that affects nearly all companies together — a recession, a rate shock, a war. No amount of diversification within equities removes it.

The split matters because it sets a floor. Adding holdings reduces specific risk toward zero, and does essentially nothing to market risk. Someone holding every share in the world still carries the risk that shares as a class fall.
How many holdings does it take? The literature disagrees, and the disagreement is worth knowing.

Evans and Archer, in the Journal of Finance in 1968 (volume 23, pages 761 to 767), found that the reduction in variability flattened out quickly — around ten stocks captured most of the available benefit. That produced the rule of thumb, still widely repeated, that eight to ten holdings is enough.

Statman challenged it directly. In the Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis in 1987 (volume 22, pages 353 to 363), in a paper titled How Many Stocks Make a Diversified Portfolio, he argued that a well-diversified portfolio of randomly chosen shares needs at least 30 for a borrowing investor and 40 for a lending one — several times the accepted figure.

The two studies were not measuring quite the same thing, which is why both can be defensible. Asking when the risk-reduction curve flattens gives a small number. Asking when the remaining benefit stops being worth the cost of not diversifying further gives a larger one. A review of this literature published in 2021 found the question still unsettled after five decades. When a number is repeated as settled and the literature says otherwise, the repetition is the thing to distrust.
Counting holdings is in any case the wrong question, because holdings can be far less independent than they look.

An investor owns twenty companies. All twenty are banks. The count says diversified; the exposure says one bet on one industry, and in a banking crisis they will fall together. Twenty holdings across twenty unrelated industries is a different portfolio with the same number of names.

The same applies across countries. Holding only companies from your own country is called home bias, and it is close to universal — investors everywhere hold far more domestic equity than the size of their market would justify.
The tendency to hold a much larger share of domestic companies than their weight in the world market would suggest.

The concern is not patriotism. It is that your salary, your house and your pension are already exposed to your national economy. Concentrating your equities there too stacks several bets on one outcome, and Chapter 3 covers why correlated bets are the ones that hurt.

Diversification also does the least when it is needed most. In a severe downturn, correlations across companies, sectors and countries rise together — the things that normally move independently start moving as one. The protection is real in ordinary conditions and weakest in the crisis it was bought for. Chapter 5 shows this happening.

The practical version is short. Spread across industries and countries, not just across names. Expect it to reduce the risk of one company failing, not the risk of a bad decade. And treat any confident number of holdings as a rule of thumb whose own literature has argued about it for fifty years.
Counting is the wrong instrument because what matters is not how many holdings you have but how independently they behave.
A measure of how closely two holdings move together, from plus one (identical movement) through zero (unrelated) to minus one (exactly opposite).

Two holdings with a correlation near one give you almost no diversification however different their names are. Two with a low correlation give you a great deal even if you own only a few. This is why twenty banks behave like one position and why an investor holding five genuinely different businesses across five industries may be better diversified than one holding thirty within a single sector.
The same reasoning gives an honest way to think about the home bias problem rather than simply naming it.

Consider what a globally diversified holding actually implies. It means accepting that most of your money sits in companies from countries you do not live in, whose language you may not read, and whose news you will not see. That is uncomfortable, and the discomfort is the reason home bias is close to universal. It is not a reason the exposure is better.

A globally diversified fund is not automatically balanced across the world either. Because most broad global indices are weighted by market value, a small number of large markets dominate. Buying the world index buys the world in the proportions the rule specifies, and those proportions are far from equal. Check the country weights before assuming global means spread.

blocks.text: What to look for when assessing whether you are actually diversified. Group your holdings by industry rather than by name and see how the totals fall. Do the same by country, and then again by currency, which is often a different answer. Add your employer and your property to the picture, since both are exposures you already hold. And ask which single event would damage the largest share of the total, because that is your real concentration whatever the holdings list says.

List everything you own that is exposed to markets, and beside each write the industry and the country. Then add your job and, if you own property, your home. Total the exposures by country. Most readers doing this honestly find that between two thirds and all of their financial life depends on one national economy, which is a fact worth knowing before deciding it is acceptable.
There is a further axis this chapter has deliberately left until now, because it sits outside equities entirely.

Spreading across industries and countries diversifies within one asset class. Market risk, by definition, survives all of it. The only remaining tool is to hold something whose returns come from a different source altogether — bonds, cash, or property — and the trade is that these have generally produced lower long-run returns in exchange for behaving differently when equities fall.

Do not assume they always behave differently. There have been periods when bonds and equities fell together, and the assumption that one reliably cushions the other is a claim about a sample rather than a law. Chapter 6 returns to this with the evidence on what correlations do in the worst months.

quiz.question: An investor holds twenty companies, all of them banks. What has diversification achieved?
options: Full diversification — twenty holdings is above the usual rule of thumb
Very little: the holdings share the same industry risk and will tend to fall together
Nothing at all; diversification never works
It has removed market risk but not specific risk
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Counting names is not the measure — what matters is whether the holdings are exposed to the same things. Twenty banks share industry risk almost entirely, so the specific risk of any one bank is spread while the risk that hits banks as a group is untouched. Note also that diversification never removes market risk, however well spread.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. The number of holdings is not what makes a portfolio diversified — their independence is. Twenty banks will tend to fall together in a banking crisis, so the count overstates the protection considerably. And diversification reduces specific risk, never market risk.

quiz.question: Why is the number of holdings a poor measure of how diversified a portfolio is?
options: Because more holdings always means more risk
Because what matters is how independently the holdings move — thirty highly correlated holdings behave like one position, while a few uncorrelated ones spread risk genuinely
Because diversification only applies across countries, not companies
Because holdings cannot be counted accurately in a fund
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Correlation, not count, determines the benefit. Twenty banks share the same exposure to rates, credit losses and regulation, so they behave as one bet. Five businesses in five genuinely different industries can spread risk more effectively than thirty in one.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. More holdings do not increase risk, and diversification applies at every level. The point is that holdings which move together provide little protection regardless of how many there are — correlation is what does the work.

quiz.question: A reader buys a single global equity index fund. What should they still check?
options: Nothing — a global fund is by definition evenly spread across the world
The country weights, because most global indices are weighted by market value and a small number of large markets dominate
Whether the fund holds bonds as well as shares
Whether the fund is priced in their home currency
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Global means the rule includes companies worldwide, not that the money is spread evenly. Market-value weighting concentrates heavily in the largest markets, so the actual country exposure can be far less balanced than the word global suggests.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. A global index fund is weighted by market value in almost all cases, which means a few large markets dominate the holding. The country weights are published, and they are the thing to check before assuming global means spread.

keyTerms.def: Risk attached to one company. Diversifiable.
Risk affecting nearly all companies together. Not diversifiable within equities.
Holding far more domestic equity than the home market's global weight would justify.

lessons.chapterTitle: Risk and Position Sizing for Equities
lessons.title: What Risk Actually Means Here
lessons.keyIdea: Volatility is movement you can wait out. Permanent loss is not. Confusing the two produces both panic selling and reckless holding.

blocks.text: Risk is used to mean several different things, and the differences decide what you should do. Two matter most, and they call for opposite responses.
How much a price moves around. High volatility means large swings in both directions.
Value that is not coming back — a company that fails, or a holding sold at the bottom and never rebought.

A diversified index fund is volatile and rarely produces permanent loss for someone who holds it. A single company can be relatively calm and then go to zero. Treating the first as dangerous and the second as safe, because one moves more, is the most common error in this whole subject.
The response differs completely. Volatility is endured. Permanent loss is avoided in advance, by not concentrating and not being forced to sell.
The fall from a previous peak to a subsequent trough, as a percentage. It describes the worst of an experience rather than its average.
Drawdown is the number people actually live through, and the arithmetic of recovering from one is unintuitive in a specific direction: losses and gains are not symmetrical.

A 20% fall needs a 25% gain to get back to even. A 30% fall needs 42.9%. A 50% fall needs 100%. A 78% fall — the Nasdaq between 2000 and 2002 — needs 354.5%. The gain required grows far faster than the loss that caused it, because it is calculated on the smaller amount that remains.
This is the arithmetic reason to care more about avoiding large losses than about capturing large gains. A drawdown that is twice as deep is much more than twice as hard to undo.

Depth is only half of it. A 40% fall recovering in eighteen months and a 40% fall recovering in eleven years are the same number and completely different lives. The second outlasts most people's patience, most people's job security, and quite a lot of people's retirement dates. Chapter 5 puts real durations on both.
The third form of risk has no bad companies in it at all, and depends only on when things happen to you.
The risk that the order in which returns arrive damages you, even when the average return is unchanged.

If you are contributing steadily, a fall early on is helpful — your later contributions buy at lower prices. If you are drawing an income, the same fall early on is severe, because you sell units at depressed prices to live on and there are fewer left to recover.

Two people retire five years apart with identical savings and experience identical average returns over twenty years. One meets a 40% fall in their first two years of drawing income, the other in their last two. The averages match exactly. The outcomes do not, and the difference is entirely the order of events.

Notice that nothing in that example is a mistake. Neither person chose wrongly. Which is the point: some risk is not the consequence of a bad decision, and the only defence is arranging things beforehand so a bad sequence is survivable.
Carry three questions into the next lesson. How far could this fall. How long could it stay down. And would I be forced to sell while it was.
The most common way risk is measured deserves scrutiny, because it is used far beyond what it can support.
A statistical measure of how widely returns have varied around their average. The usual industry shorthand for risk.

It has two limitations that matter to a reader rather than to a statistician. It treats an upward move and a downward move as equally undesirable, which no investor does. And it describes the ordinary range of variation, which is precisely not the part of the distribution that damages people.

The Foundations track established that extreme moves happen far more often than a normal distribution predicts, and the Forex track showed one in detail. A risk measure calibrated on ordinary weeks will understate the week that matters. Any statement of the form this cannot happen, it would be a six standard deviation event is a statement about the model rather than about the market.
There is also a form of risk that no statistical measure captures at all, and it is the one that ends most investment plans.

An investor holds a well-diversified portfolio through a 40% fall. Nothing they own is impaired and their time horizon is twenty years, so the fall is volatility rather than permanent loss. Then they lose their job in the same downturn, and they sell to pay for living costs. The volatility became a permanent loss at the moment their circumstances forced the sale — and the two events had the same cause.

This is why cash held outside the market is part of an equity risk plan rather than a distraction from it. Money you will not be forced to sell into a fall is what converts a drawdown from a permanent loss into a waiting period.

blocks.text: What to look for when assessing the risk of any holding. Ask what its largest historical fall was, and how long that fall lasted before recovery. Ask what would make the loss permanent rather than temporary. Ask whether anything in your own circumstances would force a sale during exactly that period. And distrust any single number offered as the risk of an investment, because the three questions above cannot be compressed into one.

For your largest holding, find the worst peak-to-trough fall it has experienced and how long it took to recover. Then write down what your monthly costs would be if your income stopped, and how many months you could cover without selling. Compare the two answers. If the recovery took longer than your reserve would last, you have found the actual risk in your position, and it is not in the price history.
One risk runs in the opposite direction to everything above, and a lesson on risk that omitted it would be dishonest.
The loss of purchasing power over time, which affects money held in cash more severely than money held in productive assets.

Cash does not fall in nominal terms, which makes it feel safe. Over thirty years, a sustained 3% inflation rate roughly halves what a fixed sum will buy. Equities are volatile and have historically compensated for inflation over long periods; cash is stable and reliably does not. Avoiding the risk you can see by accepting one you cannot is the most common error in the whole subject.

This is not an argument for holding no cash. The previous section explained why cash outside the market is what prevents a forced sale. It is an argument against treating cash as the risk-free option for money that will not be needed for decades, because for that money it is not.

quiz.question: A holding falls 50%. What gain is needed to return to the starting value, and why?
options: 50% — the same amount it fell
75%, because of compounding
100%, because the gain is calculated on the smaller amount that remains
It depends on how long the recovery takes
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. 100 falling by half is 50, and getting from 50 back to 100 is a doubling. The asymmetry grows fast: a 78% fall, which is what the Nasdaq did between 2000 and 2002, needs a gain of 354.5%. This is the arithmetic reason avoiding deep losses matters more than capturing large gains.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. The percentages are not symmetrical, because the gain is calculated on what is left rather than on what you started with. 100 falls to 50, and 50 must double to reach 100 again — a 100% gain to undo a 50% loss.

quiz.question: What are the two main limitations of standard deviation as a measure of investment risk?
options: It is difficult to calculate and rarely published
It treats upward and downward moves as equally undesirable, and it describes ordinary variation rather than the extreme moves that cause real damage
It only applies to bonds
It exaggerates risk in every market condition
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. No investor regards a large gain as a problem, yet the measure counts it as variation. More importantly, it is calibrated on the ordinary range, and extreme moves occur far more often than a normal distribution implies — so the measure understates precisely the event that matters.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. It is easy to calculate and universally published, and it tends to understate rather than exaggerate tail risk. The two real limitations are its symmetry between gains and losses, and its poor description of extreme moves.

quiz.question: An investor with a twenty-year horizon holds a diversified portfolio through a 40% fall, then loses their job and sells to cover living costs. What happened?
options: They experienced volatility only, since the portfolio was diversified
Volatility became a permanent loss because their circumstances forced a sale — and the job loss and the market fall had the same underlying cause
They made a valuation error when they first invested
The portfolio was insufficiently diversified
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Nothing they owned was impaired, so the fall was volatility for anyone able to wait. Being forced to sell removed the ability to wait, which is what converts a drawdown into a permanent loss. Because downturns cause job losses, the two risks arrive together — which is why cash held outside the market is part of an equity plan.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. The portfolio and the valuation were not the problem. The loss became permanent because a forced sale removed the option to wait for recovery, and the forced sale had the same cause as the fall itself.

keyTerms.def: How much a price moves around, in both directions.
Value that is not coming back.
The fall from a previous peak to a subsequent trough.
The risk that the order of returns harms you, even when the average is unchanged.

lessons.chapterTitle: Risk and Position Sizing for Equities
lessons.title: Position Sizing and Concentration
lessons.keyIdea: How much you hold of one thing decides how bad your worst case is. It is the one input you control completely.

blocks.text: Most attention in investing goes to what to buy. Position size — how much of it — does more to determine outcomes, and unlike the first question it has an answer you can actually compute.
How much of your total portfolio is held in one investment, usually as a percentage.
The argument is simple. You cannot control whether a company disappoints. You can control, exactly and in advance, how much that would cost you.

A company you hold falls 60% on bad results. If it was 2% of your portfolio you are down 1.2% — an ordinary week. If it was 40% you are down 24%, which needs a 31.6% gain to undo. Same company, same news, same day. The only difference was a decision made before any of it happened.

Readers of the Forex track met this in Chapter 3 Lesson 1, where sizing follows from a stop-loss distance and a fixed risk percentage. Equities need an adjustment, because the concept of a stop behaves differently here.

A stop-loss on a single company does not protect you against the event that matters most. Bad news arrives when the market is closed, and the shares reopen far below your stop — a gap, not a slide. The Forex track showed this with the Swiss franc in 2015; for a single company it happens on any results morning. Sizing so that the worst case is survivable is more reliable than a stop, because it does not depend on being able to trade.
So the equity version of the question is not where would I get out, but how much of this can I hold and still be fine if it goes to zero overnight.
Holding a large share of a portfolio in one company, industry or country.

Concentration is not automatically wrong. It is the only way to substantially beat an index, and every investor who has done so was concentrated in something. The trade-off is symmetrical and should be stated plainly: concentration raises the range of outcomes in both directions.

A portfolio of 5 equally-weighted companies has 20% in each. One failing costs a fifth of everything. A portfolio of 30 has 3.3% in each, and one failing is a bad month. The first can also produce a return the second cannot. Neither is correct in the abstract — but only one of them can be recovered from with an ordinary income and ordinary patience.
There is a second concentration most people carry without noticing, and it is usually the largest one.

Holding shares in your own employer stacks two exposures on one event. If the company fails you lose the job and the holding in the same week, at the moment you most need savings. Chapter 2 warned about correlated holdings; this is the most concentrated correlation available, and it is common because employers encourage it. Treat employer shares as part of your position sizing, not as a separate benefit.

A workable default: decide the maximum you would hold in any single company before you look at any company, and write it down. Deciding a limit while looking at a specific holding you are enthusiastic about is not deciding a limit.
The number itself matters less than having one. Anything that keeps a single failure inside the range of an ordinary bad month is doing the job.
The rule is easier to keep if you convert it into the number that actually matters: what a total failure would cost you.

A portfolio of 50,000 with a maximum single position of 2% means 1,000 in any one company. If that company falls 60%, the loss is 600, or 1.2% of the portfolio. If it fails completely, the loss is 1,000, or 2%. Both are recoverable within an ordinary year, which is the test the limit exists to pass.
Sizing a position is a decision made once. Keeping it sized is a decision made repeatedly, because success itself breaks the rule.
The growth of a successful holding into a larger share of the portfolio than was ever chosen, simply because it rose.

A holding bought at 2% that rises fivefold while the rest is flat becomes roughly 9% of the portfolio without any decision having been taken. The investor did not choose a 9% position. They chose a 2% position and then did nothing, which is how most large concentrations are actually acquired.

Trimming a winner feels like a mistake and is emotionally the hardest routine action in investing. It is also the only way a limit survives success. Chapter 4 gives this a formal shape as a rebalancing band, so the decision is made by a rule written in advance rather than in the moment when the holding is up 400% and you feel unusually clever.

blocks.text: What to look for in your own portfolio. Calculate each holding as a percentage of the total, not in currency, because currency amounts conceal proportions. Identify the largest one and write down what a total loss of it would do. Check whether any position is larger than you would deliberately choose to buy today at that size. And add up your holdings by industry, since three positions of 8% in the same industry is a 24% position wearing three names.

Work out what percentage of your portfolio your largest holding represents. Then ask a single question: if it went to zero tomorrow, would this be a bad month, a bad year, or a changed life? If the answer is the third, the size is wrong regardless of how good the company is, and no amount of confidence in it changes that.
The rule is tested hardest in the opposite direction to drift, when a holding falls and the temptation is to buy more of it.
Buying more of a holding after its price has fallen, reducing the average price paid.

Averaging down is defensible when the reason for owning the company is unchanged and the position stays within its limit. It is not defensible as a way to recover a loss, and the two are almost impossible to tell apart from the inside. The distinguishing test is whether you would open the position at this size today, knowing nothing about what you paid before.

A holding that has fallen is already a smaller share of the portfolio, so adding to it feels like restoring the intended size. It is not the same thing. Restoring a weight is a rule applied to everything you own; adding to one falling company because it fell is a decision about that company, and it needs the same evidence any new purchase would need.

quiz.question: Why is position sizing often more important than which company you choose?
options: Because company analysis is worthless
Because you control size exactly and in advance, while you do not control whether a company disappoints
Because larger positions always produce larger returns
Because sizing eliminates risk
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Size is the input you set precisely before anything happens; performance is the one you cannot. The same 60% fall is an ordinary week at a 2% weight and a 24% portfolio loss at 40%. Note that a stop-loss is a weak substitute here, because bad news gaps the price before you can act.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. Analysis is worth doing and larger positions do not reliably produce larger returns — they widen the range in both directions. The point is control: you decide size exactly and in advance, while you cannot decide whether the company disappoints.

quiz.question: A holding bought at 2% of a portfolio rises fivefold while everything else is flat, reaching roughly 9% of the total. What has happened?
options: The investor made a deliberate decision to increase the position
The position drifted to a size that was never chosen, which is how most large concentrations are acquired
The portfolio has become better diversified
The holding must now be sold entirely
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. No decision was taken; the market took it. This is position drift, and it is why keeping a limit requires periodic action rather than a single choice at purchase. Chapter 4 turns that action into a rebalancing band so it is governed by a rule written in advance.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. Nobody chose the 9%, which is exactly the problem — and drift concentrates a portfolio rather than diversifying it. The remedy is not necessarily a full sale but a rule that restores the intended size.

quiz.question: A portfolio of 50,000 caps any single holding at 2%. What is the maximum that one company failing completely can cost?
options: 1,000, which is 2% of the portfolio
600, because companies rarely fall to zero
10,000, since concentration risk compounds
It cannot be calculated in advance
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. 2% of 50,000 is 1,000, and total failure costs exactly that. The point of sizing is that this number is knowable and fixed before anything happens, which is what makes it the one input an investor controls completely.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. The whole purpose of a size limit is that the worst case is known in advance: 2% of 50,000 is 1,000, and a complete failure costs that and no more. A 60% fall would cost 600, but the maximum is the full position.

keyTerms.def: How much of a portfolio is held in one investment.
Holding a large share in one company, industry or country.

lessons.chapterTitle: Risk and Position Sizing for Equities
lessons.title: Dollar-Cost Averaging vs Lump Sum
lessons.keyIdea: Investing gradually loses to investing at once about two thirds of the time. It is a tool for managing regret, not returns — and that is a legitimate use.

blocks.text: Someone with a sum to invest faces a choice that feels much harder than it is: put it in now, or spread it over months. The evidence has a clear answer, and the clear answer is not the whole story.
Investing a fixed amount at regular intervals, so more units are bought when prices are low and fewer when they are high.
Investing the whole amount at once.

First, a distinction that causes most of the confusion. Someone investing 200 a month from their salary is not choosing a strategy — they are investing money as it arrives, which is the only option available. The debate applies only to someone holding a sum now and deciding how quickly to deploy it.

For that person, Vanguard's research — published under the title Dollar-cost averaging just means taking risk later — found that investing the lump sum immediately outperformed spreading it out roughly two thirds of the time.

The reason is unglamorous. Markets rise more often than they fall. Money waiting to be invested is not invested, so it misses the rises more often than it dodges the falls. Averaging in is, in expectation, a decision to hold cash for a while.

Spreading a sum over twelve months means that on average only about half of it is invested during that year. If the market rises over the period — the more common outcome — the uninvested half earned nothing. The strategy did not fail; it did exactly what it promised, and what it promised was less exposure.

Two thirds of the time is not always. In the third of cases where the market falls after the investment date, averaging in does better, sometimes substantially. Anyone presenting lump sum as simply correct is describing an average as a certainty — the same error the value-premium lesson warned about.
So why does averaging in survive as advice? Because the return-maximising choice and the choice someone can actually stick to are not always the same.

Investing everything the day before a 30% fall is a specific and memorable experience. It produces the feeling that you did this, which is what makes people sell at the bottom and stay out for years. That reaction has a cost, and the cost is often larger than the expected advantage of investing at once.

Two investors put in a lump sum and see it fall 25% within a month. The first, who chose lump sum after understanding the trade-off, holds. The second, who was talked into it, sells and does not return for four years. The second investor's decision to invest at once was correct on the evidence and disastrous in practice.

This is why the honest framing is not which is better but what is this for. If the aim is expected return, invest at once. If the aim is reducing the chance of an abandonment you cannot undo, averaging in buys that at a known and modest expected cost.

Averaging in must have an end date decided in advance. Without one it becomes indefinite hesitation with a respectable name — and the person spreading a sum over six months and the person who has been about to invest for six months look identical from outside. Write down the schedule before starting.
A behavioural tool is a real tool. Sizing a decision so you can live with it is not a failure of nerve; it is the same reasoning as the previous lesson, applied to time instead of amount.
The mechanism is easier to trust once you have seen it run in both directions, so here it is with numbers.

An investor has 12,000 and spreads it over twelve monthly purchases of 1,000. Suppose the price starts at 100, falls to 75 by month six, and recovers to 105 by month twelve. The schedule buys about 134.7 units at an average price of about 89.11, worth about 14,139 at the end. Investing all 12,000 at the start buys 120 units, worth 12,600. Averaging in won, because the low prices arrived while money was still being deployed.

Now run the same schedule in a market that rises steadily from 100 to 122. The monthly purchases buy about 108.5 units, worth about 13,241 at the end. The lump sum buys 120 units, worth 14,640. Averaging in lost, by more than it won in the first example, because the money not yet invested missed a rise that was happening the whole time.

Those two examples are the entire debate. Averaging in wins when prices fall during the schedule and loses when they rise, and prices rise more often than they fall. That is where the two-thirds figure comes from, and neither example is evidence of anything except the mechanism.

Note what neither example contains: any information available at the start. The investor in the first example was not clever and the one in the second was not careless. They made the same decision and met different markets, which is why the choice has to be made on expected value and on what you can hold to, not on what happened to somebody.

blocks.text: What to look for when deciding for yourself. Establish first whether you are actually facing this decision, or simply investing a salary as it arrives, in which case there is no choice to make. If you do hold a sum, decide the schedule and its end date before the first purchase. Ask honestly what you would do if the market fell 25% in month two, since the strategy is worthless if you would stop. And treat the expected cost of averaging in as the price of a behavioural guarantee, which is a fair thing to buy.

Write down the sum you would invest, the number of months you would spread it over, and the date of the final purchase. Then write one sentence describing what you will do if prices fall sharply during the schedule. If that sentence says you would pause, rewrite the plan as a lump sum, because a schedule you would abandon at the low point delivers the cost of averaging in without the benefit.
One cost of averaging in is easy to overlook and straightforward to control.

Twelve purchases instead of one means twelve spreads, and where a platform charges per trade, twelve commissions. On a large sum this is trivial and on a small one it is not. Someone spreading 3,000 over twelve monthly purchases of 250 with a fixed charge per trade can lose a meaningful percentage to costs that a single purchase would have avoided.

Check the per-trade charge before choosing the number of instalments. Four quarterly purchases capture most of the behavioural benefit of twelve monthly ones at a third of the trading cost, and the difference between four and twelve instalments has very little effect on the outcome the research measures.

quiz.question: Vanguard found lump-sum investing beat dollar-cost averaging about two thirds of the time. What follows?
options: Dollar-cost averaging is a mistake and should never be used
Lump sum has the higher expected return, while averaging in reduces the chance of a regret-driven exit — a legitimate trade at a known cost
Lump sum always wins, so the timing decision does not matter
The research is unreliable because markets change
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Markets rise more often than they fall, so money waiting to be invested misses more rises than falls — that is where the two-thirds comes from. But in the other third averaging in does better, and its real value is behavioural: reducing the chance of an abandonment that costs far more than the expected difference.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. Two thirds is not always, and the remaining third is exactly when averaging in helps. The finding says lump sum has the higher expected return; it does not say averaging in is a mistake, because reducing the chance of panic-selling has real value that the average return figure does not capture.

quiz.question: An investor spreads 12,000 over twelve months while the price falls from 100 to 75 and recovers to 105, ending with about 14,139. The same money invested at once would have been worth 12,600. What does this example prove?
options: That averaging in is the better strategy
Nothing beyond the mechanism — averaging in wins when prices fall during the schedule, and prices rise more often than they fall
That the investor timed the market successfully
That lump-sum investing is unsuitable for volatile markets
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Run the identical schedule against a market rising from 100 to 122 and averaging in finishes at about 13,241 against 14,640 for the lump sum. Neither outcome was knowable in advance, and since markets rise more often than they fall, the average case favours investing at once.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. A single favourable path is not evidence about the strategy. The same schedule loses in a rising market, and rising is the more common outcome — which is exactly why the research finds lump sum ahead about two thirds of the time.

quiz.question: Someone plans to average a sum in over twelve months but admits they would pause the schedule if the market fell 25% in month two. What should they do?
options: Proceed, since pausing during a fall is prudent
Recognise that a schedule they would abandon at the low point gives them the cost of averaging in without the benefit, and reconsider the plan
Extend the schedule to twenty-four months
Switch entirely to cash until the market is calm
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The benefit of averaging in comes precisely from continuing to buy while prices are low. Stopping at the low point removes the benefit and keeps the cost — the money that missed the rises. The plan needs to be one they would actually follow, or it is not a plan.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. Pausing feels prudent and is the opposite of how the strategy works: the cheap purchases are the entire mechanism. A longer schedule makes the problem larger, and moving to cash abandons the decision rather than making it.

keyTerms.def: Investing a fixed amount at regular intervals.
Investing the whole amount at once. Higher expected return, higher regret risk.

lessons.chapterTitle: Risk and Position Sizing for Equities
lessons.title: Margin, Leverage and Short Selling
lessons.keyIdea: Borrowing removes limited liability, and shorting removes the floor. Both convert a bad outcome into one that can exceed what you put in.

blocks.text: Everything so far assumed you invest money you have. Two common practices break that assumption, and both undo protections earlier lessons relied on.
Borrowing from a broker to buy more shares than your cash allows, using the shares themselves as collateral.
Margin multiplies the outcome in both directions, and the multiplication is straightforward.

You have 10,000 and borrow another 10,000, buying 20,000 of shares. A 20% rise makes 4,000 on your 10,000 — a 40% return before interest. A 20% fall loses 4,000, which is 40% of your money. The shares moved 20%; you moved 40%.

Lesson 1 said limited liability caps your loss at what you paid. Borrowing removes that cap. The loan is owed regardless of what the shares do, so a large enough fall can leave you owing money after the position is gone. An investment that cannot cost more than you put in is a different thing from one that can, and margin converts the first into the second.
There is also a mechanism that can force the loss to be realised at the worst possible moment.
A demand from the broker for more money when the collateral value falls too far. If it is not met, the broker sells your holdings to repay the loan.

This is what turns a temporary fall into a permanent loss. Chapter 3 Lesson 1 distinguished volatility, which you can wait out, from permanent loss, which you cannot. A margin call removes the ability to wait — the position is closed at the bottom, by someone else, and any later recovery happens without you.
Forex Chapter 3 Lesson 2 covered the same mechanism in that market. The instrument differs; the sequence does not.
Short selling inverts the position entirely.
Borrowing shares, selling them, and hoping to buy them back cheaper before returning them. A bet that the price falls.

The asymmetry from Lesson 1 now runs against you, and it is worth stating precisely. A share you own can fall to zero — you lose what you paid, and no more. A share you have shorted can rise without limit, and every unit of rise is your loss.

You short 100 shares at 50, receiving 5,000. If the price goes to zero you keep the 5,000 — that is the maximum possible gain. If it rises to 250 you must buy back at 25,000, losing 20,000 on a position that received 5,000. There is no level at which the loss stops.

A short can also be closed against your will. The lender can recall the borrowed shares at any time, forcing you to buy back immediately whatever the price. If many shorts are forced to buy at once, their buying drives the price up, forcing more of them to buy — a short squeeze. Chapter 5 examines the most famous recent example, and finds the popular explanation of it does not survive contact with the regulator's own report.

Shorting also carries an ongoing cost. You pay to borrow the shares, and on a heavily shorted company that fee can be substantial — so the position loses money while nothing happens, and being right eventually is not the same as being right in time.

Neither tool is illegitimate. Both are used competently by professionals every day. The point is that both remove a protection the rest of this track has been relying on, and neither belongs in a beginner's portfolio.
It is worth knowing how far a price has to move before a margin call arrives, because the answer is much closer than most borrowers assume.
The minimum proportion of a margined position that must be covered by your own money. Fall below it and the broker demands more or sells.

You put in 10,000, borrow 10,000, and hold 20,000 of shares. The maintenance requirement is 25%. Your equity is the value of the shares less the 10,000 loan, so the call arrives when the position is worth about 13,333 — a fall of just 33% in the shares. At that point your own money is down to about 3,333, a loss of two thirds, and the broker can sell without waiting for you.

A 33% fall is common. It is smaller than the fall in either case study in Chapter 5, and smaller than several ordinary corrections. Leverage does not create a distant catastrophic scenario; it converts an unremarkable market event into a forced sale at the worst available price.
The equivalent constraint on a short position is the cost of holding it, and that cost is not fixed.
The annual rate charged for borrowing shares to short. It rises with demand and can become extreme on a company many people want to short.

A short of 5,000 with a borrow fee of 20% a year costs 500 to hold for six months, before any price movement. If the shares are unchanged after six months, the position has lost 10% of its value doing nothing at all. On a heavily shorted company the rate can be far higher.
